en: The Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by Kumārajīva, Tripiṭaka Master of Kucha during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great [assembly].
The assembly of bhikṣus numbered sixty-two thousand;

and there were seventy-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—renowned throughout the world—who had all gathered from the worlds of the ten directions. They had attained dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence, entered into mindfulness and wisdom, and were fully endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame. Their resolve was as firm as adamant, and they had skillfully cultivated and perfected all Buddha-dharmas. With pure intentions, they were fully accomplished, never forgetting their own bodhicitta and enabling others likewise not to forget it.
They were well-disciplined and gentle in their giving, having mastered the subduing of the sense faculties and being skilled in relinquishing all cherished things.
They adorn themselves well with pure precepts, maintaining a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings;
they adorn themselves with the power of gentle patience;
and they diligently cultivate the power of exertion throughout immeasurable nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
He sports with mastery and unimpeded freedom in all meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and supernatural powers;
he skillfully uses wisdom to discern the words and meanings of all phenomena;
his mind is as immovable as the king of great mountains; and toward all sentient beings his mind is impartial, like earth, water, fire, and wind, perfectly free from attachment and aversion.
Constantly practicing a mind of loving-kindness, they perpetually dispatch rays of compassion;
illuminating all sentient beings everywhere, they abide in great compassion;
constantly and diligently observing all sentient beings, they dwell in the fulfillment of the Dharma of great sympathetic joy.
Abiding in great equanimity, one attains non-dual wisdom;
gain and loss, defamation and fame, praise and blame, suffering and pleasure—all such worldly dharmas are transcended.
With the light of wisdom, one skillfully subdues both one's own assembly and that of others, and overcomes all Māras.

As rare as the udumbara flower to encounter in the world, he lets out the great lion’s roar among all sentient beings; he has attained ultimate nirvana and possesses the profound, supreme four fearlessnesses, being sealed with the seal of the Tathāgata;
his predictions are never erroneous, and he acts exactly as he speaks; he is in accord with the meaning and flavor of the profound treasury of Dharma;
he eclipses the sun and moon, and his fame spreads throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
If one is protected and sustained by all Buddhas, guarding the treasury of the Dharma so that the lineage of the Three Jewels is never interrupted;
being able to travel freely through boundless Buddha-fields;
and skillfully understanding and knowing how to serve and attend to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as appropriate, while listening to and receiving the Dharma;
They are constantly diligent and energetic in teaching and transforming sentient beings, having reached the further shore of skillful means and wisdom;
they skillfully accord with the faculties of all sentient beings and preach the Dharma accordingly;
and they skillfully know the mental activities and dispositions of all sentient beings.
With a mind that is pure, wondrous, and skillful in speech, he acts as a great physician-king who effectively cures all ailments;
he has planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* Buddhas;
and he has excellently accumulated the merit of the primary and secondary marks as his adornment.
They are skillfully able to understand emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

they are skilled in understanding that all phenomena are like illusions, like mirages, like the moon reflected in water, and like dreams or images in a mirror, and they understand that all phenomena have the characteristic of space;
they are skillfully able to understand the voices and speech of all sentient beings.
They possess inexhaustible eloquence in skillfully discerning the joy of the Dharma;

they are adept at investigating supramundane wisdom, achieving great power that approaches the ten powers of a Buddha; they obtain clarity regarding the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye;
and they are skilled in the means of adornment for the factors that assist the path.
He is skillfully able to deliver beings across all paths and clearly understands that which is encompassed by the Bodhisattva Dharma-treasury;
he is adept at turning the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma and has attained the seal-mark of samādhi;

he is skilled in knowing the Samādhi of Reaching the Vajra-Sphere and the Samādhi of Sovereignty over All Dharmas, both of which are constantly present before him; he holds the great jewel-torch, his mind is humble toward all sentient beings, he constantly observes the minds of all sentient beings and also constantly observes the wisdom of all sentient beings, drawing near to the wisdom of the Buddha, and causing all sentient beings to perform the work of Buddhas.
Having already gathered all that was to be accomplished, their merits—extending through all future kalpas—could not be fully exhausted even if one were to speak of them for an eternity.
Their names are:
Bodhisattva Ratnasthita, Bodhisattva Ratnasat, Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, and Bodhisattva Ratnapuṣpa.
Bodhisattva Ratnarāja, Bodhisattva Priyadarśana, Bodhisattva Priyāśaya, Bodhisattva Priyanayanadarśana,
Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara, Bodhisattva Priyakara, Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Bodhisattva Mahāguṇa, Bodhisattva Mārajit,
Bodhisattva Makutadatta, Bodhisattva Brahmadatta, and Bodhisattva Māndārava.
Gandhahastin Bodhisattva, Satyarata Bodhisattva, Samantadarśin Bodhisattva, Anunnatāvanata Bodhisattva, Susārthavāha Bodhisattva,
Sarvasattvāparyādāyaka-mitra Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Meghasvara Bodhisattva,
Merudhvaja-vyūha Bodhisattva, Merukūṭa Bodhisattva, and Varuṇadeva Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Brave Friend, the Bodhisattva Radiance, the Bodhisattva Glorious Virtue, the Bodhisattva Lamp King, the Bodhisattva Observing Resolve,
the Bodhisattva Adorned with Light, the Bodhisattva Variegated Crown, the Bodhisattva Celestial Crown, the Bodhisattva Celestial King,
the Bodhisattva Observing with the Celestial Eye, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, and the Bodhisattva Good...
the Bodhisattva Bāhu, the Bodhisattvas Cittaśrī and others, the Bodhisattva Supratiṣṭhitamati, the Bodhisattva Supratiṣṭhitakarma,
the Bodhisattva Akampyacaraṇasaṃcaya, the Bodhisattva Vajracaraṇavikrama, the Bodhisattva Trailokyasamatikrāntacaraṇa,
the Bodhisattva Kṣiprapratibhāna, the Bodhisattva Śīghrapratibhāna, the Bodhisattva Anupacchinnapratibhāna, and the Bodhisattva Vihārin...
The Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, the Bodhisattva Brahmakalpa, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana,
the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, and others such as these, numbering seventy-two thousand, were the leaders of the assembly.

In this trichiliocosm, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors, along with other deities of great majesty and power—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, have all gathered together, desiring to hear the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands who paid him respectful homage as he expounded the Dharma.

Then, the Bodhisattva Tiānguān rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse:
"Transcending the world, you act as a lamp for the world; With wisdom, you bring benefit to the world."
May those bound in darkness obtain illumination; I now bow my head to you who have transcended the world.
Your practice of giving throughout the ten directions is most supreme; having well disciplined your own mind, you have reached the other shore.
Honored by humans, devas, nāgas, and spirits, I bow my head in reverent salutation to the Benevolent One who has incinerated all fetters.
With supreme marks that greatly benefit the world, A golden hue and a circular halo pervading everywhere;
Upholding pure and wondrous precepts with a most beautiful voice— I bow my head to the peerless one in the three realms.
Having ferried all sentient beings to the other shore, Subduing all treatises so that none can move you;
Thoroughly understanding the minds of all sentient beings— I bow my head in reverent salutation to the Supreme Great Compassionate One.
Having severed all fetters and afflictions, he gives rise to no attachment; with power he subdues enemies and dwells well in the precepts.
The God among Gods has purified the stains of his fetters; I prostrate and pay homage to him who has subdued all foes.
Most stainless among all jewels, always delighting in wisdom as the foremost;
having severed the defilements of greed, hatred, and delusion, I bow my head to the one whose mind is equal to space.
Proclaiming the Four Truths to cross over the four floods, Expounding the nectar-like Dharma to bestow the pure eye;
Wandering through the three realms for the benefit of all beings— I prostrate with my head to the one who bears the mark of the wheel.
Constantly receiving offerings from humans and devas, Constantly transforming sentient beings to bring them across to liberation;
Like space, receiving offerings from humans and devas— I prostrate and pay homage to the Supreme among Men.
Always delighting in gathering the true and wholesome dharmas, always treating the world with a heart of universal compassion;
Honored among men, the Tamer who abides in the Right Path—to you who uphold all virtues, I bow my head.
The sublime and excellent goodness spoken by Pure Sound, with a pleasing, supple, and Brahma-like voice;
you who skillfully understand all sounds and have reached the other shore—to you who speak with such exquisite truth, I prostrate.
You who proceed toward emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, And who can [perceive] the most profound and difficult-to-see Dharma;
You who are well able to advance and enter liberation— I bow my head to you, the one who well knows the path to liberation.
The World-Honored One skillfully understands and knows causes and conditions, Always able to sever and depart from the views of the two extremes;
Truly expounding the retribution of karma through causes and conditions, I bow my head in prostration to the Seer of the World.
There is neither one who comes nor one who goes; free from pride, you are well able to contemplate all phenomena.
Like a phantom, like a mirage, like a reflection in water—to you with the excellent Dharma-eye, I prostrate in reverent salutation.
If birth were non-birth, there would be no birth at all; if there were birth and cessation, there would likewise be no cessation.
His place of abiding is to dwell in accordance with the Dharma; thus does the Tamer dwell well in such a place.
All your speech is true; you dwell securely in suchness, impervious to being shaken.
With a body like a mountain of vajra, you are unshakable; I prostrate to you who are impervious to being shaken.
His body, speech, and mind are equal and without distinction; his fame is immeasurable, pervading the three realms.
I now wish to question this supreme man; may the Honored One not hesitate, but explain it for me.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Tiānguān (Cūḍāmaṇi) had praised the Buddha with verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to ask a few questions regarding the supreme and wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; if the Buddha grants me permission, I shall venture to inquire.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Tiara-Crown: "Good son!
Ask whatever you wish; according to your doubts, the Tathāgata shall speak so as to gladden your heart."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tiānguān addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva achieve eloquence adorned with various kinds of ornaments?”
"Bhagavān!
How does a bodhisattva attain superior wisdom and skillfully know and discern the most profound dharmas?
Bhagavān!"
"How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the various faculties?
World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva skillfully understand and know how to preach the Dharma as is appropriate?"
"Bhagavān!
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the mental activities of all sentient beings?
Bhagavān!"
"How does a bodhisattva know all causes, actions, and their karmic retributions, and how does he also know how to transcend what is practiced without error?
World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva adorn generosity?"
"Bhagavān!
How does a bodhisattva adorn morality, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom?
Bhagavān!"
"How does a bodhisattva skillfully understand and know the adornment of the Brahma-path?
World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva not lose their supernormal powers?"
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva sever all fetters and latent tendencies?
World-Honored One!”
"How does a bodhisattva cross over to the other shore?
World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva can manifest the physical forms, colors, and dignified demeanors of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and sentient beings without any distinction?"
"Bhagavān!
How does a bodhisattva contemplate birth-and-death (saṃsāra) while not dwelling in nirvāṇa?
Bhagavān!"
"How does a bodhisattva contemplate the realm of sentient beings while remaining unmoved within the dharma-realm?
World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva, without retreating from their benefit, contemplate the manifestation of apparent loss?"
World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva possesses inexhaustible great wealth and fiefdoms, yet through the power of skillful means manifests as poor?
World-Honored One!
"How does a bodhisattva practice among all conditioned activities so as to enter the gate of non-action through the gate of action?
World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva skillfully contemplate all dharmas?"
"Bhagavān!
How does a bodhisattva definitively discern all dharmas?
Bhagavān!"
"How does a bodhisattva practice all worldly dharmas without being defiled by them?
World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva not look to others for authority among all those who possess power?"
"Bhagavān!
How does a bodhisattva not become separated from seeing the Buddha? Bhagavān!"
"How does a bodhisattva skillfully discipline themselves so as to be free from all unwholesome dharmas?
World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva skillfully act as a teacher and guide without being stingy with the Dharma?"
"Bhagavān!
How does a bodhisattva serve as a true refuge for all sentient beings?
Bhagavān!"
"How does a bodhisattva enable the turning of the wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas?
World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva attain the stage of consecration regarding all dharmas?"
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Tiānguān:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
"What you have now asked brings great benefit and peace to the world, bringing welfare and security to humans and devas, and encompasses all future bodhisattvas.
Well done, son of good family!"

You have frequently inquired and posed difficult questions before as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; now, once again, you shall bring great benefit and peace to future bodhisattvas, ensuring that this Mahāyāna remains long in the world.
“Good son! Listen attentively with a virtuous mind to what you have asked; I shall now expound it for you.
Devapūrvaka Bodhisattva replied:
“World-Honored One!
We shall listen with reverence. “Good son!”
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will attain the eloquence of manifold adornments.
What are these four?
This bodhisattva harbors no intent to harm toward any sentient being, and relinquishes all cherished possessions with a mind free from regret or stinginess.
When there is a teacher of the Dharma who does not cease his preaching, one should give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, rejoice with exuberant delight, and praise him, saying, "Excellent!
One should entreat him to continue teaching the Dharma.

Whether by day or night, whether in the midst of the Saṃgha or at a Buddha-stūpa, one should always take the bodhicitta as the foremost path, giving rise to a mind of aspiration and taking joy in all dharmas.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva focuses his mind and will, bestowing gifts through the Dharma without expecting gain or honor.
Son of good family!
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves eloquence adorned with various kinds of ornaments.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they attain superior wisdom and skillfully know how to discern the most profound teachings.
What are these four?
By following the law of dependent origination, one knows my true nature;
one knows how to enter the true nature of all sentient beings;
and one knows that in the process of birth and death, there is neither one who comes nor one who goes.
To know that all phenomena bear the mark of the seal of emptiness—
this is the fourth. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they skillfully know the faculties.
What are the four?
They skillfully know the gateway to the dharma-realm.
They contemplate all dharma-gates without obstruction;
they know all supernormal powers;
their minds are well-tamed, free from dualistic activity.
These are the four. "Good son, when a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas,
he is well able to understand and know how to preach the Dharma as is appropriate."
What are the four?
The wisdom of eloquence;
the wisdom of delivering sentient beings.
To discern the knowledge of dharmas;
to purify one's own mind and also purify the minds of all sentient beings—
these are the four.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, he will skillfully know the mental activities of all sentient beings.
What are these four?
Their wisdom transcends all knowledge and is without obstruction;
they enter into skillful means,
and in all that they do, they never experience regret midway.
To be able to awaken to this for oneself—
this is the fourth. "Good son!

When a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they skillfully understand the karmic retributions resulting from the causes they create, and they also know how to transcend them so that their conduct remains faultless.
What are these four?
They do not propound annihilationism, nor do they propound eternalism.
One knows the retribution of karma as it truly is, and manifests the signs of all phenomena in accordance with the Dharma.
Within this, there is no self and nothing belonging to a self.
One knows that what has been done does not lose its fruit and retribution.
These are the four. "Good son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they adorn their giving."
What are the four?
Adorning the primary marks;
adorning the secondary characteristics.
Incomparable physical form;
inexhaustible fiefdoms and the jewel-hand—
these are the four.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they adorn their observance of the precepts.
What are these four?
He becomes a wheel-turning monarch and thus well-adorns the bodhicitta;
he becomes Śakra-devānām-indra and thus well-adorns the bodhicitta;
he becomes Mahābrahmā and thus well-adorns the bodhicitta.
Not falling into the evil realms, but being born in the good destinations of humans and devas, one thus skillfully adorns the bodhicitta.
These are the four. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they adorn patience.
What are these four?
Producing the voice of Brahmā and the voice of the kalaviṅka bird.
Beloved by many, with a joyful mind,
he firmly cultivates wholesome dharmas and attains golden-hued skin.
These are the four. "Good son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, his adorned diligence becomes indestructible."
What are the four? They are:
attaining a state such that no sentient being can destroy them; acting as an uninvited friend to all sentient beings;
being single-minded and tireless in whatever they undertake; and having a mind free from weariness or fatigue.
Delighting in the accumulation of extensive learning and adorning oneself with firm wisdom—
these are the four.
“Good son! A bodhisattva who is untiring accomplishes four dharmas to adorn meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). What are these four?
Being free from all clamor and distraction.”
They are without negligence,
without stinginess or pride,
and do not abandon the mind of self-discipline.
These are the four. "Good son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they adorn their wisdom."
What are the four?
Not speaking of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life span;
and attaining unimpeded eloquence.
They are well able to discern the meaning of all phrases and sentences;
they have no doubts or perplexities regarding any phenomena. These are the four.
“Good son! A bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas to adorn the Brahma-path.
What are these four?
One gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness in a state of empty purity.
One gives rise to a mind of compassion for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
One gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy for the sake of protecting the True Dharma.
To give rise to the wisdom of the Tathāgata by generating a mind of equanimity—
this is the fourth. "Good son!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will not lose their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
What are these four?
Entering the four dhyānas without falling back or losing them.
Entering the four formless absorptions, they know the skillful means;
with the mind attaining mastery, they know all dharmas;
through their supernormal powers, they travel to immeasurable Buddha-fields.
These are the four. "Good son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, he severs all fetters and latent tendencies."
What are the four? They are:
being inwardly tranquil and also tranquil outwardly;
skillfully contemplating all phenomena and knowing them to be like illusions and transformations.
They possess the power of great wisdom,
not the power of pride.
These are the four.
“Good son! A bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas to reach the other shore.
What are the four?
He knows that he has not yet realized freedom from desire regarding the flood of sensual desire;
he knows that he will be reborn at will regarding the flood of existence;
and he knows that he does not abandon various views regarding the flood of views.
To know that the flow of ignorance does not turn back from its conditions is the fourth. "Good son!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they can manifest the physical forms, colors, and dignified demeanors of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and sentient beings without any distinction.
What are these four?
He skillfully gives rise to the illusion-like samādhi,
knows the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are,
and skillfully contemplates the five supernormal powers.
To observe one's own body and know it to be like a magical illusion—
this is the fourth. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they contemplate birth and death without dwelling in nirvana.
What are these four?
They are being protected and sustained by all Buddhas.
From great compassion,
through skillful means,
and without abandoning their original vows.
These are the four. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, he contemplates the realm of sentient beings without wavering from the dharma-realm."
What are the four?
Contemplating the true nature of oneself;
understanding the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
To contemplate the nature of sentient beings without doubting the nature of wisdom;
and to contemplate that all sentient beings share the same nature as nirvana—
these are the four.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, he does not regress from his loss of benefit, even when currently experiencing a loss of benefit.
What are these four?
"Good son! With a single-minded resolve, you should direct yourself toward nirvana while practicing within the cycle of birth and death."
To single-mindedly aspire toward all Buddha-dharmas while manifesting as śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas to discipline sentient beings—
this is the fourth.

“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, he possesses great wealth, treasures, and fiefdoms that are inexhaustible, yet through the power of skillful means, he manifests as one who is poor and destitute of all riches.
What are the four?
Sometimes he manifests as a great universal monarch (cakravartin), Śakra, or Brahmā, in order to transform and uplift those beings who are most exalted.
He manifests as one who is impoverished, in order to transform and uplift those beings who are impoverished.
Seeing those who come seeking, one completely relinquishes all possessions and wealth.
Seeing those who are very wealthy, one manifests inexhaustible treasures and displays sovereign power.
These are the four.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, he causes the gate of conditioned activity to enter the gate of unconditioned non-activity.
What are these four?
It is taught that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
one purifies the course of wisdom and attains the realization that all conditioned phenomena are without self.
To be free from all views, to attain the Dharma of nirvāṇa,
and to proceed with the wisdom of tranquility— these are the four. "Good son!..."
When a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they skillfully observe all phenomena.
What are these four?
They are the thoroughly purified eye of wisdom.
One attains the clear Dharma-eye;
the Buddha-eye manifests before one;
and one attains the stage of empowerment regarding all phenomena.
These are the four. "Good son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they definitively discern all phenomena."
What are the four? They are:
the analytical knowledge of eloquence;
and the knowledge of the truths through unimpeded comprehension.
Abiding in the wisdom of the four reliances and not abandoning the wisdom of dhāraṇī—
these are the four.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, he engages in worldly dharmas without being defiled by them.
What are these four?
Observing and knowing the phenomena of the world,
they transcend and surpass the sentient beings of the world;
having severed craving and aversion, they remain undefiled.
It is ultimately luminous and pure;
these are the four. "Good son!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will attain mastery over all phenomena and not look to others for guidance.
What are these four? They are:
attaining mastery over meditative concentration.
They have attained mastery over wisdom;
they have attained mastery over insight;
they have attained mastery over skillful means.
These are the four. "Good son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, he is never separated from seeing the Buddha."
What are the four?
One goes oneself to see the Buddha and also encourages sentient beings [to do so].
One goes oneself to listen to the Dharma and also encourages sentient beings [to do so].
To personally resolve for bodhicitta and to also exhort sentient beings to resolve for bodhicitta,
and to never abandon the *nien-fo* samādhi—
these are the four.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, he will skillfully subdue himself and be free from all unwholesome dharmas.
What are these four?
With supramundane, luminous wisdom, they observe with insight and vision,
manifesting liberation and skillfully accumulating the patience for the Dharma.
To sever and abandon all habitual tendencies toward unwholesome dharmas—
this is the fourth. "Good son!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will skillfully serve as a guide and teacher without being stingy with the Dharma.
What are these four? They are:
to single-mindedly benefit all sentient beings; and to maintain a firm resolve without any resentment.
They constantly practice the transformation of all sentient beings;
having relinquished their own pleasure, they cultivate and accumulate wisdom,
always acting for the benefit of all sentient beings as their own fulfillment of self-interest.
These are the four. "Good son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, he serves as a true refuge for all sentient beings."
What are the four? They are:
relinquishing one's own benefit while constantly seeking the benefit of others;
and personally renouncing all forms of pleasure in order to seek the joy of the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
To extensively expound the Dharma as one has heard it for others without weariness;
to sustain one's life through the Dharma rather than through food and clothing—
these are the four.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, he is able to turn the wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas.
What are these four?
They attain dhāraṇīs;
they attain unceasing eloquence and knowledge;
and they enter into the mental activities of all sentient beings.
He teaches the Dharma without regard for their lineage, leading them into nirvana.
This is the fourth. "Good son!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they attain the stage of empowerment regarding all dharmas.
What are these four?
They transcend all conditioned activities and abide in the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Having attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they manifest birth and death;
sealed by the seal of non-retrogression, they enter the seal of the Tathāgata;
abiding in the tenth stage, they skillfully know all the stages.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves the stage of consecration regarding all dharmas.
When the Buddha had spoken these various sets of four dharmas, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and a great light shone everywhere.
In the sky above, hundreds of thousands of billions of devas performed celestial music and sang hymns of praise, raining down *mandārava* flowers, and uttered these words of exultation:

"The unsurpassed, true, and correct path of the Dharma, accumulated by the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, has been entirely revealed and expounded herein within these four dharmas."

If there are sentient beings who hear this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and furthermore transcribe it, and explain it in detail within the great assembly, you should know that such persons have not come from meager merit.

If there are sentient beings who hear such four-line verses as these, and having heard them, believe, understand, uphold, read, and recite them, and widely explain them for others among the great assemblies without departing from the bodhicitta, those people will before long let out the great lion’s roar within the great assemblies of humans and devas, just as the Tathāgata now lets out the great lion’s roar.

We have now gained a great and wholesome benefit in that we have been able to hear such four-line verses of Dharma, and furthermore, we are able to believe, understand, and expound upon these fourfold teachings.

At that time, eighty-four thousand devas and humans resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpāda-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tiānguān addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

By accomplishing how many dharmas can a bodhisattva, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, hear this sutra, receive, uphold, read, recite, and also transcribe it, and further expound and reveal it extensively within the great assembly?"
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Tianguan: "Good son,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they shall, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, uphold, recite, and transcribe this sutra, and explain it in detail within the great assembly."
What are the eight? They are:
the accomplishment of resolute intent directed exclusively toward bodhi;
and the ultimate practice of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, being free from any intention to harm them.
Abiding in great compassion, he transforms all sentient beings.
He constantly seeks the benefit of the Dharma, delights in the Dharma, desires the Dharma, seeks the Dharma, and gathers the Dharma; his mind knows no satiety, like the ocean swallowing all streams.
They relinquish their bodies and lives to protect the True Dharma;
they plant thick roots of goodness and accumulate all manner of merit;
they give rise to great vows which are sustained by all Buddhas.
Subduing all Māras and enemies, and being free from fear among the great assembly.
Heavenly Crown!

These are the eight dharmas by which a bodhisattva, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, is able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and transcribe such a sūtra-dharma, and extensively explain it for others within the great assembly.

When this Dharma was being expounded, this trichiliocosm likewise shook in six ways; the pits, mounds, mountains, and impurities, as well as the rivers, streams, and great oceans, all ceased to appear, yet they did not disturb or harm the sentient beings dwelling in the waters.

At that time, the great trichiliocosm was entirely level like the palm of a hand and exquisitely adorned. Within this great trichiliocosm, all trees that had withered for a hundred years sprouted flowers and leaves and leaned toward the Buddha; likewise, all growing plants, trees, flowers, leaves, and fruits flourished and also leaned toward the Buddha.

Upon this great earth, various lotus flowers have grown, as large as chariot wheels, of diverse and lovely colors, with exquisite fragrances that are pleasing to the mind and a great radiance that shines everywhere throughout this trichiliocosm.

In the void above, there were various devaputras who, without manifesting their forms, played a multitude of musical instruments. Hearing the sound of this music, all the devas dwelling within the King of Snowy Mountains and the King of Fragrant Mountains produced exquisite fragrances in double measure, causing this great trichiliocosm to be entirely filled with a pervasive, great fragrance.

At that time, from the King of Snowy Mountains and the King of Fragrant Mountains, a rain of various wondrous flowers fell, all flowing toward the Buddha and filling the trichiliocosm. All other trees likewise rained down flowers. In the sky above was a single precious canopy covering ten thousand yojanas; this great precious canopy was adorned with hanging strings of pearls and nets of bells. From within these nets of bells, sounds emerged that were soft and pleasing to the mind, and a great, sublime voice was heard throughout the trichiliocosm.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, seeing this miraculous manifestation, joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!
What auspicious omen of light is this? There is such a rare and unprecedented sign that this entire trichiliocosm is universally adorned and exceedingly delightful."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"This is the Great Tree Kinnara King!

From Mount Gandhamādana, surrounded by a great assembly of immeasurable kinnaras, immeasurable gandharvas, immeasurable devas, and immeasurable mahoragas, he wishes to come to see the Buddha, pay homage, and make offerings."
"This is the sign that the Great Tree Kinnara King is about to come to see the Buddha.

Before these words had even faded, the Great Tree Kinnara King arrived, surrounded by a vast multitude of immeasurable kinnaras, gandharvas, devas, and mahoragas. They performed eighty-four thousand musical instruments, blending them with pure and wondrous songs in perfect harmony.

Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings all followed along; sustained by the great power of the Bodhisattva’s supernormal faculties, they ascended into the air, raining down various flowers everywhere as they approached the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, together with his retinue, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and stood before the World-Honored One.

At that time, the Great Tree Kinnara King, using his own lapis lazuli lute—which was adorned with leaves and flowers of Jāmbūnada gold and fashioned from the ripening of pure karma—skillfully tuned it before the Tathāgata, along with eighty-four thousand other musical instruments.

When this Great Tree Kinnara King plucks this lute and beats upon the various musical instruments, its sound will be heard throughout this entire trichiliocosm; the resonance of this lute and the exquisite voice of song will completely overshadow the music of all the devas in the realm of desire.
At that time, all the devas belonging to the desire realm abandoned their musical instruments and came to where the Buddha was.
When the great Kinnara King Druma played the lute, all the groves and mountains within the trichiliocosm—
including Mount Sumeru, Mount Himavat, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, and Mount Kāla, as well as all medicinal herbs, trees, and forests— suddenly surged upward and then sank back down.

It surged, gradually surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere; it shook, gradually shook everywhere, and shook equally everywhere; it quaked, gradually quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere—just as if a person were extremely intoxicated with wine, staggering forward and backward, unable to support themselves, so too did the various mountains and Mount Sumeru surge and submerge in such a manner!

When the Great Tree Kinnara King played the lute, among the Buddha’s great assembly—consisting of kings and their retinues, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the World Protectors, humans, non-humans, and those free from desire—with the exception of those bodhisattvas who were non-retrogressive, all the other members of the great assembly, upon hearing the sound of the lute and the various musical instruments, could not remain still and rose from their seats to dance.

At that time, the entire assembly of śrāvakas, unable to endure the sound of the lute music, each rose from their seats; casting aside their dignified deportment and composed appearance, they gave way to unrestrained pleasure, like children dancing and playing, unable to restrain themselves.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Diademed spoke to all these great śrāvakas, Mahākāśyapa and the others:

"Virtuous ones, you have already abandoned the afflictions, attained the eight liberations, and seen the Four Noble Truths; why do you now each abandon your dignified deportment and move your bodies about in dance like those small children?"
At that time, the venerable śrāvakas replied: "Good son!
Within this matter, we have no autonomy."
For what reason?
Because of this lute music, each of us is unable to sit at ease; our bodies move and dance, unable to maintain self-control, and we cannot cause our thoughts to remain settled.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tiānguān (Cūḍāmaṇi) addressed the Venerable Kāśyapa, saying:

"How is it that you, O Elder, who possess few desires and are content, who practice the dhūta austerities and always delight in emptiness and stillness, and whom devas, humans, and asuras revere like a stupa—how is it, Venerable One, that you cannot maintain your body and instead dance like a small child?"
"Why do you say that not protecting [them] is for the sake of the great assembly's mind?
Mahākāśyapa replied,
"Good son!..."

Just as a great whirlwind blows upon trees, medicinal herbs, and thickets, they lack the power to maintain themselves in stability; though this is not what their original nature desires or delights in, they are nonetheless agitated and cannot hold themselves steady.
"Noble son!

Now this Great Tree Kinnara King beats upon his lute with music and harmonizes it with wondrous songs; the sounds of the flutes and pipes stir my heart so that I cannot hold myself steady, like trees swayed by a whirlwind."
The power of the vows, merit, and spiritual majesty of this virtuous man is superior to all the majestic virtues possessed by the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tiānguān (Makuṭadhara) said to Mahākāśyapa:
"Behold now the majestic power of these non-retrogressive bodhisattvas; even the sound of those lute melodies cannot cause them to waver or be startled."
Venerable Kāśyapa!
Who, upon seeing such as this, would not resolve to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true bodhicitta? Why is this so?

Now, the power and majesty possessed by my immeasurable wisdom are not equal to the sound of this lute; for even such persons of great majestic virtue cannot maintain their composure upon hearing this lute, yet those who are irreversible from the Mahāyāna cannot be moved by it.

At that time, the Great Tree Kinnara King readjusted his lute and eighty-four thousand other musical instruments. Sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and the power of the Great Tree Kinnara King’s own past roots of goodness, the sounds of all the lutes and instruments spoke these verses:
“All phenomena tend toward tranquility, Whether they be superior, middling, or inferior;
Empty, still, and extinguished, free from affliction, The stainless and supreme now manifests.”
All sentient beings are, in truth, no sentient beings; this is likewise true for the past and the present.
To cause the multitude to hear, one speaks by means of sounds; these sounds are equal and identical to the Dharma-realm.
All worlds are equally worldless; phenomena are explained as having the characteristics of space.
Without arising, without increase, and without decrease, they are revealed as false and illusory like space.
The Buddhas are all equally awakened; the dharma-realm is determinate and indestructible.
Understanding and penetrating generosity, morality, and wisdom, they are of one mark, equal and identical to the signless.
All fetters are stilled and eternally absent; yet deluded thought gives rise to discrimination therein.
There is no internal, no external, and no middle; they exist only through the inversion of deluded thought.
If one has no delusive thoughts regarding what is dharma or non-dharma, and seeks all dharmas and finds them to be non-existent;
having realized the true nature of name-and-form as it is, such a person acts in the world without defilement or attachment.
The past and future are boundless in measure, and the Dharma taught is likewise so;
its original limit is quiescent and inexhaustible, having no location and no place of abiding.
These dharmas are taught by means of words and letters, yet these words and letters are themselves of the nature of exhaustion;
having realized that these words and letters are of the nature of exhaustion, one is free from conceptual proliferation regarding all dharmas.
Maintaining the mind in meditative equipoise, there is nothing to be grasped; self and other do not contradict the characteristics of phenomena.
Mind and its mental factors have no arising; knowing all phenomena, one enters into equality.
The limit is itself limitless; there is nothing to be severed. In the beginning, middle, and end, they are equally unattainable.
Having realized that the three periods of time are equal, That wisdom is boundless and immeasurable.
The world is greedily attached to name-and-form; Whether finite or infinite, all is quiescent.
Having realized the characteristics of the dharma of dependent origination, There are no delusions of self, sentient beings, or a life-principle.
The view of self that arises never arises again, and all phenomena likewise do not arise;
if that which arises is fundamentally non-arising, one is always in accord with the patient acceptance of the nature of phenomena (dharmakṣānti).
Its nature is like lightning in the clouds; all phenomena are like my true nature.
The natures of self, person, and sentient beings are inherently empty; enter this seal-mark of the dhāraṇī.
According to the realization of the three gates of liberation— The single characteristic, the signless, and their identical nature;
All existent phenomena are boundless and immeasurable, And within each phenomenon, there is inherently no delusive conceptualization.
One explains the differentiated dharmas through words—whether superior, middling, or inferior;
yet words themselves are devoid of conceptual construction, for one seeks and discerns the true meaning.
Meaning and words are in mutual correspondence; through sound, the non-dual meaning is proclaimed.
If one knows that the fundamental nature is eternally quiescent, that primordial limit is eternally severed of its own accord.
If the nature of the primordial limit is eternally severed of itself, one cultivates all practices for the sake of benefiting the world;
seeking the primordial limit, one finds no such limit—this great compassion is most pure.
If one’s great compassion is most pure, practicing with equanimity toward both suffering and joy,
neither exalting nor disparaging others— such a person is called a Great Being who knows the benefit.
The Dharma-eye is tranquil, supremely tranquil; whether seeing or not seeing, it is eternally tranquil.
It neither increases nor decreases; its nature is free from activity and eternally tranquil.
Just as a sound in the sky cannot be grasped, though it may be heard and known, yet cannot be described;
so too, both the speaker and the listener are entirely unreal and lack any independent existence.

When these verses and the sounds of the Dharma were performed by the lutes and musical instruments, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tiara-Crown addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
“From where do such wondrous verses emerge?
The Buddha said, “Good son!”
"You should now ask the Great Tree Kinnara King yourself;
he shall answer you.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Tiara asked the Great Tree Kinnara King:
“Kinnara King! From where do such sublime verses emerge?
He replied:
“Good son! It emerges from the sounds of all sentient beings.
He asked again:
“From where do the voices of all sentient beings arise?
He replied, “Good son!
"The voices of sentient beings emerge from empty space.
The Bodhisattva Tiānguān asked, "Kinnara King! Why is this so?"
“Is it not the case that the voices of sentient beings do not issue from the mouth? He replied: “Good son!
"Does this sound of sentient beings emerge from the body, or does it emerge from the mind?
Tianguan replied,
"It does not emerge from the body, nor does it emerge from the mind."
Why is this? The body is deluded and ignorant, like grass, wood, tiles, or stones;
the mind has no form or color and cannot be seen, it possesses no tactile resistance and cannot be described, being just like a magical illusion.
The Kinnara Mahādruma said:
"O son of good family!
If one is separated from body and mind, from what would [the voice] emerge?"
The Heavenly Crown replied,
“Sound is produced from reflection.
He asked again:
"If there were no space, from what would sound emerge? Tianguan replied,
"If there were no space, sound would ultimately not emerge."
The kiṃnara said: "Good son! Therefore, you should know that all sounds emerge from space;

you should know that these sounds are of the nature of space. Having been heard, they immediately cease; once ceased, they abide as the same as the nature of space. Thus, whether dharmas are spoken or not spoken, they are identical to the nature of space. For this reason, one should not abandon the limit of emptiness."
Just as it is with the division of sounds, so it is with all dharmas!
If one preaches the Dharma by means of sounds, these dharmas cannot be found within the sounds, nor can the sounds be found within the dharmas.
"Good son! For this reason it is said:
'All dharmas are ineffable; it is only by means of sound that they are called "expressed. "
"You should know that what is called 'speech' is actually nothing spoken; furthermore, speech is designated by means of sound.
Yet this sound has no place of abiding from the very beginning.
That which has no place of abiding lacks solidity, and thus it is called 'reality'."
If it were real, it could not be destroyed;
if it cannot be destroyed, it does not arise;
and if there is no arising, there is no cessation.
If there is no cessation, this is called purity.
If it is pure, it is then white and clean;
if it is white and clean, it is then stainless.
If it is stainless, it is luminosity;
if it is luminosity, it is the nature of the mind;
if it is the nature of the mind, it is transcendence.
If one transcends, then one transcends all marks;
if one transcends all marks, that is the state of true reality (bhūtatathatā);
if a bodhisattva abides in this state of true reality, they are said to have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
If one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one is able to endure all things; one endures both emptiness and the person (*pudgala*). Why is this?
Because one does not depart from the person when designating it as empty; the person is itself emptiness.
One endures the signless and also endures signs.
Why is this? Because the true nature of these signs is itself the signless.
One endures both the wishless and the wishful.
Why is this? Because the true nature and characteristic of a wish is itself the wishless.
The nature of all phenomena and the nature of sentient beings are likewise always extinguished; such is the patience [of the bodhisattva]. Why is this?

The nature of birth and death of all sentient beings is like an illusion or a dream; this is called the bodhisattva’s attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Not contradicting any dharma and not opposing any dharma—if one accords with this patience, then one also patiently accords with and follows all dharmas;
if there is no going, then there is no coming;
if there is neither going nor coming, one knows that all dharmas are of a permanently abiding nature, just as the Dharma abides permanently, and sentient beings are likewise so!

If one attains this state, practicing in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with that state, this is called the accomplishment of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

All verbal expressions are merely sounds; these sounds arise for the purpose of communicating to others. However, regarding this patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, there is neither one who can speak it nor one who can hear it.
Why is this? Because this meaning cannot be apprehended; furthermore, this Dharma-patience is neither sound nor speech. "Good son!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses great majestic power; he is identical with the meaning of non-attainability, yet he speaks of attainment within the meaning of non-attainability.
*Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Fascicle One.
*Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tiānguān addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!
It is unprecedented that this Great Tree Kiṃnara King has accomplished such inconceivable dharmas.”
"Bhagavān!
This Kinnara King is indeed able to accomplish such supreme and wondrous power of supernatural faculties, and further, he is able to expound upon the profound dharma-patience."
“World-Honored One!
Under how many Buddhas did the Kinnara King plant roots of goodness to possess such eloquence?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Suppose one were able to count the stars in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; one could not count the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas served by this Kinnara King.”

Good son! This person has already practiced the pure conduct under as many Buddhas as there are, and has accumulated the path of unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment; for this reason, they possess such eloquence.
At that time, Devamukha asked the Kinnara King:
"Since you have planted immeasurable and boundless roots of goodness under so many countless Buddhas, for what reason have you not attained the unsurpassed, right path?"
At that time, the Great Kinnara King Druma said to the Bodhisattva Māukuṭa: "Good son,
there are twelve dharmas of non-satisfaction for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
What are these twelve? They are:
never being satisfied in making offerings and serving the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
and never being satisfied in accumulating roots of goodness.
They never tire of listening to the collection of the Dharma-treasure;
they never tire of practicing meditative concentration and liberation;
they never tire of practicing the dharma of tranquil contemplation.
There is no satiety in circulating and manifesting the Dharma;
there is no satiety in teaching and transforming sentient beings;
there is no satiety in protecting the true Dharma.
He never tires of not abandoning forest hermitages;
he never tires of adorning buddha-fields through the various pāramitās;
and he never tires of cultivating and accumulating merit and wisdom.
There is no satiety in gathering the factors that assist toward enlightenment.
Son of good family!
These are called the twelve dharmas of non-satiety for a bodhisattva; therefore, a bodhisattva never reaches satiety in seeking the adornment of roots of goodness.
At that time, the Great Kinnara King Druma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have heard that there is a samādhi possessed by bodhisattvas called ‘Jewel Abiding’ (Ratnasthiti).”
If there are bodhisattvas who attain this samādhi, they will spontaneously acquire all the jewels of the Dharma and all dharmas of merit.
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
We only pray that the Tathāgata will expound upon this Ratnākara-samādhi, so that bodhisattvas, having heard it, may attain mastery over all dharmas and cause those dharmas to increase accordingly."
At that time, the Buddha said to the Great Kinnara King Druma:
"So it is, Kinnara King!"
There is a samādhi called Ratnasthiti.
Listen well now and reflect upon it carefully; I shall now expound this Bodhisattva Ratnasthiti Samādhi.
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We wish to hear it with joy; we shall receive your instruction and listen.
The Buddha addressed the Great Tree Kinnara King:

“If there are bodhisattvas who wish to ensure that the lineage of the Buddha-jewel is not severed, and that the lineages of the Dharma-jewel and the Sangha-jewel are not cut off, they should cultivate and give rise to eighty kinds of jewels.”
What are these eighty? They are:
not forgetting the jewel-mind of omniscience;
not abandoning the jewel-mind of resolute intention.
The jewel-like mind that does not abandon the cultivation of all roots of goodness;
the jewel-like mind that does not abandon the firm entry into tranquil meditative concentration;
and the jewel-like mind that gives rise to all forms of giving.
The jewel-mind of purity that does not hope for recompense, because it dedicates [merit] toward bodhi;
the jewel-mind that adorns the body, because it fulfills the three types of wholesome action;
the jewel-mind that adorns speech, because it is free from the four faults.
The jewel-mind that adorns the intention is so called because it abandons ignorance, craving, hatred, and views.
The jewel-mind of upholding precepts—unbroken, unpierced, unimpaired, and flawless—is so called because it is adorned with precepts that are unpierced, unimpaired, flawless, and unstained.
The jewel-mind free from affliction and harm, because it maintains equanimity toward all sentient beings;
the jewel-mind of gentle patience, because it is able to endure difficult matters;
and the pure jewel-mind that does not worry about body or life, because it purifies bodhi.
The jewel-mind free from attachment and aversion, because it is without high or low.
The jewel-mind firm, stable, and strong, because it is without anxiety or concern.
The jewel-mind that accomplishes all undertakings, because it is without laxity or negligence.
One enters the jewel-mind of firm mindfulness and wisdom, because one is able to skillfully cultivate and accumulate the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
One gives rise to the jewel-mind of dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi, because one attains mastery over the mind.
The mind that accumulates the treasure of the Dharma, because it gathers one's own wealth;
the mind that upholds the treasure after hearing the true Dharma, because it attains fearlessness;
and the mind that does not begrudge the treasure of the Dharma, because the mind is free from stinginess.
The jewel-like mind of teaching the Dharma without expectation of gain or support, because it abandons evil desires and does not hope for recompense;
the jewel-like mind of right mindfulness, because it flows toward the correct stream;
and the jewel-like mind of fulfilling the Dharma as it has been heard, because one practices according to what was heard.
The jewel-mind of wisdom-observation, because it subdues through wisdom;
the jewel-mind of great kindness, because it transforms sentient beings;
the jewel-mind of great compassion, because it contemplates sentient beings.
The jewel-like mind of great joy, because it delights in the Dharma;
the jewel-like mind of great equanimity, because all phenomena are quiescent;
the jewel-like mind that does not weary of saṃsāra, because it accumulates all roots of goodness.
The jewel-mind of transforming sentient beings, because it does not abide in self-pleasure;
the jewel-mind of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), for the sake of gathering [beings] through the Dharma;
and the jewel-mind of giving rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), because all supernormal powers manifest transformations.
The jewel-like mind of virtuous friends, for the sake of hearing the Dharma;
the jewel-like mind of distancing oneself from evil associates, for the sake of accumulating roots of goodness;
and the jewel-like mind of practicing correctly for the sake of all sentient beings, in accordance with nirvāṇa.
The jewel-like mind that is free from all fetters and diseases, because it enters into the aspirations and desires of all sentient beings;
the jewel-like mind that conceives of all phenomena as medicine, because it pacifies all illnesses.
The jewel-mind of well-cultivated learning without pride, because it knows the dharma of the great beings;
the jewel-mind that extinguishes arrogance, because it is humble and lowly toward all sentient beings.
The jewel-mind free from illusion and deceit, because it is without flattery or deception;
the jewel-mind of harmony and respect, because it causes the Dharma to abide for a long time;
the jewel-mind that protects the Dharma, because it repays the kindness of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
The precious mind that knows and repays kindness, because it brings friendship to ultimate fulfillment;
the precious mind that expects no recompense, because it has no [selfish] attachments;
the precious mind that always leaves the household life, because it does not forget what must be done.
The jewel-mind that delights in and loves [the Dharma], because it protects purity;
the jewel-mind of the noble lineage of few desires and contentment, because it gathers and maintains the precepts;
and the jewel-mind that adorns all *dhūta* virtues, because it is free from transgression toward all sentient beings.
The jewel-like mind of few desires and contentment, for wisdom is insatiable;
the jewel-like mind of dwelling alone, for body and mind are tranquil;
the jewel-like mind of seeking the Dharma without weariness, for the purpose of perfecting the marks and signs of a Buddha.
The jewel-mind of insatiable accumulation of adorned wisdom, because it severs all doubts of all sentient beings;
the jewel-mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, because it never departs from seeing the Buddha;
the jewel-mind of mindfulness of the Dharma, because it never departs from hearing the Dharma.
The mind that recollects the Jewel of the Sangha, because it does not regress from the Bodhisattva Sangha;
the mind that recollects the Jewel of the Precepts, because it does not abandon the bodhicitta;
the mind that recollects the Jewel of Renunciation, because it relinquishes the fetters and afflictions.
The jewel-mind of mindfulness of the heavens, because it is bound to the stage of a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood;
the jewel-mind of analytical eloquence regarding meaning, because it awakens to all meanings;
the jewel-mind of analytical eloquence regarding the Dharma, because it does not destroy the dharma-realm.
The jewel-mind of eloquence in speech, because it awakens to the understanding of all sounds and voices;
the jewel-mind of joy in teaching, because it brings delight to all sentient beings;
the jewel-mind of dhāraṇī, because it does not forget or lose any Dharma that has been heard.
Relying on the jewel-mind of meaning, because one knows the true nature of syllables;
relying on the jewel-mind of wisdom, because one knows that cognition is like an illusion;
relying on the jewel-mind of definitive sūtras, because there is no conflict within the definitive meaning.
The jewel-mind of the Dharma, because it realizes the true nature of persons;
the jewel-mind of the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), because it does not abide within the three realms.
One should cultivate the jewel-like mind that contemplates all phenomena as being without self, for both oneself and sentient beings are equally devoid of self.
One should cultivate the jewel-like mind that contemplates nirvana as tranquility, for it is ultimate stillness.
The jewel-like mind that contemplates the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—because it enters the gateway to the deathless.
The jewel-like mind that contemplates the non-arising of all phenomena, because it attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.
They perceive all phenomena as being like an illusion, a dream, a mirage, a shadow, an echo, the moon reflected in water, and a jewel in the mind, because they do not abide in any views.
The jewel-mind that accords with the Dharma-treasure of dependent origination, because it is free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism;
the jewel-mind free from the defilements of all extreme views, because it is free from duality;
the jewel-mind that enters the gate of non-dual dharmas, because it awakens to the single path.
The jewel-mind that transcends all conditioned activities, because it reaches the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*);
the jewel-mind that correctly contemplates the status of phenomena (*dharmatā*), because all phenomena are equal;
the jewel-mind that gathers the auxiliary factors for all qualities of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), because it brings to awakening the realization of all Buddha-dharmas.
Thus it is, O Kinnara King!

If there are those who cultivate and assemble such dharmas as these—excellently cultivating, excellently practicing, and dwelling correctly to attain practice in accordance with what has been taught—this is called the Bodhisattva’s Jewel-Dwelling Samādhi.
If one can act in this way, one will then attain this Jewel-Abiding Samādhi (*ratnasthiti-samādhi*).
If there is a bodhisattva who has already attained the Jewel-Abiding Samādhi, yet possesses neither worldly jewels nor supramundane jewels, that bodhisattva does not attain mastery.
“Kinnara King! What is a worldly treasure?
And what is a supramundane treasure?”
Kinnara King!

As for the treasures of the world, they are said to be the noble and honored ones among humans and devas—namely, the noble Śakra, the noble Brahmā, the noble World-Protectors, the noble Cakravartin kings, the noble householders, the noble brahmins, the noble elders, and the noble kṣatriyas. Although one may attain such noble and honored status among humans and devas, one must not be heedless.
Because through heedfulness one can gather all factors conducive to enlightenment, it is called a worldly treasure.
What is called a supramundane treasure?
It is the noble wisdom that is supramundane.
Why is this? Because wisdom completely encompasses all supramundane dharmas; therefore, it is said that entering the gate of prajñā-wisdom is called "supramundane. "Kinnara King!
Just as the great ocean is the sovereign of all streams;
as Mount Sumeru is the king of all mountains;
and as the moon is the lord of all the stars.
Just as among all medicinal herbs and fire-gems, the light of the sun is supreme;
among all birds and beasts, the lion is supreme;
and among all the common people, the king is supreme.
Among the thirty-three gods, Śakra is the foremost;
among all the Brahmā deities, the Brahmā King is the foremost.
It is even so, O Kinnara King!

All supramundane dharmas have wisdom as their foremost; therefore, it is said that Prajñā is the sovereign among all sūtras, for it can ferry one across the various torrents and is the path of peaceful departure.
It is called a torch, because it illuminates the darkness of the fetters;
it is called courageous and valiant, because it eliminates all enmities.
He is called a King of Physicians because he harmonizes all medicines;
he is called a Teacher because he knows all scriptures;
he is called an Arrow because he shoots at the target of the fetters.
This is called "power," because it ultimately destroys the fetters;
this is called a "great elephant," because it uproots the trees of the knots;
this is "without conflict," because all things are equal.
This is because it is without contention and without litigation;
this is called non-opposition, because it is skillfully compliant;
this is called freedom from anger, because it is ultimately exhausted.
This is called "skillful knowledge," because it thoroughly understands the Four Noble Truths;
this is called "mindfulness," because it consists of the foundations of mindfulness;
this is called "correctness," because it is capable of right abandonment.
This is called manifestation, because of the power of supernormal faculties;
this is called precept, because it restrains the sense faculties;
this is called subjugation, because of possessing great power.
This is called awakening, because it is the skillful awakening of knowledge;
this is called revealing, because it reveals the right path;
this is called tranquility, because it is the stillness of meditative concentration.
This is called "clarity," because it produces the light of wisdom;
this is called "producing clarity," because it removes obscurations and veils;
this is the arrival at the state of correctness, because it acts as illumination.
This is called "eradication," because it eliminates the dust of the fetters;
this is "without waves," because it crosses over all currents;
this is "unseeable," because it transcends the sphere of sensory objects.
This is without objective realm, for it is free from the internal and external.
This is called emptiness, for it is free from the "this shore" of views;
this is called signlessness, for it is free from applied and sustained thought.
This is called "wishlessness," because it transcends the characteristics of the triple world.
This is called "one characteristic," because it is devoid of characteristics;
it is the characteristic of space, because it has no counterpart.
This harms craving and pride because it distances one from the deeds of Māra.
One gives without false conceptualization, not relying on precepts, not dwelling in patience, not initiating vigor, and not being stained by attachment to dhyāna.

The gate of non-discourse, the absence of all gates, self-constructed through skillful means; without self and without sentient beings, crossing over to the other shore, gathering all roots of goodness, without action and without an agent, transcending all paths of activity.
Kinnara King! This is what is called the supramundane jewel.
All the jewels of prajñā are the jewels of wisdom; they are the very essence of the Jewel-Abiding Samādhi.
If a bodhisattva attains the Jewel-Abiding Samādhi (*ratyavasthāna-samādhi*), all manner of jewels will gather together. "Kinnara King!
It is like the great ocean, which is the lord of all streams and gathers all treasures; all manner of jewels come to it for refuge, and from within this ocean, all kinds of jewels are produced."
Thus it is, Kinnara King!
When a bodhisattva attains this Jewel-Abiding Samādhi, they become the sovereign of all sentient beings, gather all jewels, and all the jewels of the Dharma flow toward them.
Kinnara King!

The Jewel-Abiding Samādhi (*ratyavyūha-samādhi*) is able to gather the jewels of all dharmas; therein, the lineage of the Three Jewels is never severed. This Jewel-Abiding Samādhi is called "the gathering of the jewels of all dharmas."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tiānguān addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Has this Great Tree Kinnara King already attained this Jewel-Abiding Samādhi?”
The Buddha said: "Good son!
You should now ask the Great Tree Kinnara King yourself!"
"I shall explain it for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tiara immediately asked the King of the Kinnaras, Mahādruma:
"King of the Kinnaras!"
"Have you now already attained this Bodhisattva Jewel-Abiding Samādhi?
He replied, "O Noble Son!"

Within this samādhi there is no abiding and no attainment; within this samādhi there is no one who attains. Furthermore, this samādhi is not form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

This samādhi cannot be seen as form, nor can it be heard as sound; it is neither a characteristic of abiding nor a characteristic of cessation. It has no characteristic of location; it is neither without characteristics nor of a single characteristic.
As for what is called "characteristic," it is entirely without characteristic and incapable of performing any action.
As for the characteristic of samādhi, it is itself without characteristic, yet it is not non-characteristic; this characteristic of samādhi should be cultivated in such a manner.
"Good son!
This samādhi is equal to all dharmas; if it is equal to all dharmas, it is also equal to me; and if it is equal to me, it is likewise equal to all sentient beings."
Therefore, good son!
This samādhi is equal toward all sentient beings. Why is this?
All sentient beings are the mark of emptiness, and the mark of emptiness is the mark of samādhi;
all sentient beings are the mark of signlessness, and the mark of signlessness is the mark of samādhi;
all sentient beings are the mark of wishlessness, and the mark of wishlessness is the mark of samādhi.
All sentient beings and all phenomena are characterized by quiescence; this characteristic of quiescence is the characteristic of samādhi.
All sentient beings are characterized by selflessness; this characteristic of selflessness is the characteristic of samādhi.

Regarding the characteristics of samādhi: it cannot be contacted by the body, nor can it be contacted by the mind; whether dharmas that can be contacted are equal or unequal, they are all expounded for the sake of being well-tamed and subdued.
Then the Bodhisattva Tiara (Devamukuṭa) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
That this Great Tree Kinnara King, while dwelling in such heedlessness, is nevertheless able to expound the most profound and wondrous Dharma."
The Buddha said, “Good son!
A bodhisattva is born from the stage of wisdom and skillful means, manifesting all actions while remaining undefiled by those very actions.”
"Good son! This is the Great Tree Kinnara King!

By means of the music of this lute, the sounds of various flutes and pipes, and his wondrous singing voice, he has subdued seventy billion kinnaras and caused them to abide in Bodhi; thirty billion gandharvas have been disciplined in the Unsurpassed Way; and eighty-four thousand of his inner retinue have abided in omniscience."
He possesses such great wisdom of skillful means, good son!
I declare this:
"This is called a bodhisattva who, wherever he dwells—whether in a great place or any other location—benefits sentient beings in great numbers."
"Good son! Just as fire does not burn in the absence of fuel,
so it is, good son!"
It is likewise with a bodhisattva dwelling in tranquility; they are unable to fervently teach and transform sentient beings.
Good son! It is like a great pile of firewood: only then does the fire blaze forth intensely.
Good son! It is the same for the bodhisattva;
he dwells amidst a great multitude, teaching and exhorting with fervent zeal. Good son!
"Therefore, you should know that when a bodhisattva dwells in the most eminent and honored position, they bring great benefit to sentient beings wherever they are born.
The Bodhisattva Tiānguān (Crown-Adorned) again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"This is the Great Tree Kinnara King!"
"How do you teach and transform sentient beings by means of the lute, exquisite singing, and the sounds of various musical instruments?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Tianguan:
"Good son!..."
The *kiṃnaras*, *gandharvas*, and *mahoragas* delight in music.

This Great Tree *Kiṃnara* King skillfully tuned his lute and harmonized with the various musical instruments; consequently, the hosts of *kiṃnaras*, *gandharvas*, and *mahoragas* gave rise to great joy and devotion, increasing their faith and respect.
Having attained this joy, faith, and increased respect, from within those sounds there issued forth the voice of the Buddha and the Dharma.
The sound of the Dharma, the sound of the Saṅgha, the sound of not forgetting the bodhicitta, the sound of generosity, the sound of ethical discipline,
the sound of patience, the sound of diligence, the sound of meditative concentration, the sound of wisdom, the sound of loving-kindness, the sound of compassion, the sound of sympathetic joy,

the sound of equanimity, the sound of the applications of mindfulness, the sound of the right efforts, the sound of the bases of psychic power, the sound of the faculties, and the sound of the powers.
The sound of awakening, the sound of the Path; the sound of concentration, the sound of wisdom, and the sounds of dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi;
the sound of impermanence, the sound of suffering, and the sound of non-self;
the sound of tranquility; the sounds of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the sounds of non-arising, non-origination, and non-conditioning; and the sound of Bodhi.
The sound of the Dharma gathered within the treasury of the *saddharma*; the sound of the fulfillment of the samādhi of the vajra-words of *dhāraṇī*;
the sound of the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma; the sound of the King of Dharma who is certain in all things;
the sound of the ocean-adornment samādhi; the sound of the samādhi of the equal flow of all dharmas; and the samādhi of sovereign mastery over all dharmas.
The sound of the Samādhi of Subtle Sound; the sound of the Samādhi of Adorned Wisdom; the sound of the Samādhi of Jewel Abiding; the sound of the Samādhi of Three Jewels;
the sound of the Samādhi of Jewel Subjugation; the sound of the Samādhi of the Jewel Torch; the sound of the Samādhi of Delight;
the sound of the Samādhi of Lotus Adornment; the sound of the Samādhi of Transcending the Lotus; and the sound of Pervading All.
The sound of the Samādhi of Abiding, the sound of the White Lotus Samādhi of All Dharmas,
the sound of the Samādhi of Augmentation, the sound of the Great Virya-vikrama Samādhi, the sound of the Lion-Virya-vikrama Samādhi, the sound of the Sun-Lamp Samādhi,
the sound of the Immeasurable Revolving Samādhi, the sound of the Forward-Advancing Samādhi, and the sound of the Vajra-maṇḍala Samādhi.
The sound of the Vajradhvaja Samādhi, the sound of the Vajrāvināśa Samādhi, the sound of the Dharaṇīdhara Samādhi,
the sound of the Giryapradīpa Samādhi, the sound of the Giryadhvaja Samādhi, the sound of the Ratnagarbha Samādhi, the sound of the Ratnapuṣpa Samādhi,
the sound of the Ratnacittavibhu Samādhi, and the contemplation of all sentient beings.
The sound of the samādhi of the mind; the sound of the samādhi that increases all practices; the sound of the samādhi of profound and firm cultivation;
the sound of the samādhi of diverse eloquence; the sound of the samādhi of non-contemplation; the sound of the samādhi of contemplating all sentient beings;
the sound of the samādhi of playful sport; and the sound of the samādhi that issues forth the realm of all supernormal powers.
The sound of the Samādhi of Subduing the Realm of Māra; the sound of the Samādhi of Manifesting All Forms;
the sound of the Samādhi of Entering All Samādhis; the sound of the Samādhi of Dividing All Bodies; the sound of the Samādhi of Abiding in All Practices;
the sound of the Samādhi of the Lamp of Wisdom; the sound of the Samādhi of the Lamp in Hand; the sound of the Samādhi of Contemplating Bodhi; and the eloquence that transcends pleasure.
The sound of samādhi, the sound of entering the samādhi of all merits. "Good son!
From among these lute songs and various musical instruments, such sounds of the Dharma of samādhi emerge, causing all sentient beings to be transformed and depart."
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish such rare and marvelous dharmas.

While this discourse on the great tree-kinnara king’s meritorious conduct and spiritual powers was being spoken, by the power of the Buddha, a mass of celestial māndārava flowers appeared, causing the great assembly to each scatter them over the great tree-kinnara king!
The Great Tree Kinnara King, using his supernormal powers, caught them with his right hand so that not a single flower fell to the ground but remained in his grasp.
Thereupon, the Great Tree Kinnara King immediately scattered them as an offering over the Tathāgata.

At the time when the flowers were scattered, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, these flowers were transformed into a single precious canopy that covered a thousand worlds. From within this precious canopy hung countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of strings of genuine pearls; from each string of pearls issued forth immeasurable tens of billions of rays of light.

From each ray of light emerged precious lotus flowers, variegated in color, exquisite, and filled with a wondrous fragrance that was pleasing to the mind. Within the calyx of every flower, the form and image of Śākyamuni Tathāgata appeared, sitting cross-legged.
Thus all these Buddhas praised the Great Tree Kinnara King:
"Excellent, excellent, Kinnara King!
You are indeed able to teach and transform immeasurable sentient beings."
