A bodhisattva should act in this manner: having transcended the world, they return to the world to teach and transform sentient beings; though their births and deaths have come to an end, they return to undergo existence; having attained the state of nirvāṇa, they still roam within the triple realm, teaching and transforming sentient beings therein.
At that time, the Great Kinnara King Druma had this thought:
"I shall now create an individual jeweled canopy for each and every Buddha to cover them."
At that time, the king immediately entered a samādhi called "Adorned Jewel Canopy.

As he entered this samādhi, exquisite jewel canopies appeared, each one covering the head of a Tathāgata. All members of the great assembly likewise held jewel canopies in their right hands, using them as their own offerings to the Buddha.
At that time, the Great Kinnara King Mahādruma again had this thought:

“I shall now invite the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, along with the bodhisattvas, the assembly of śrāvakas, and all the great multitude, to my palace on Mount Gandhamādana for a meal. I will cause immeasurable and boundless devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and others to assemble and listen to the Dharma. I myself shall serve the Tathāgata as an attendant, so that these sentient beings may obtain benefit, peace, and happiness throughout the long night.”
At that time, having formed this thought, the Great Tree Kinnara King prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms, and said:

“I pray only that the World-Honored One, together with the assembly of Bodhisattvas and the community of Śrāvakas, will take pity on us and accept our invitation to stay for seven nights at Mount Gandhamādana, so that immeasurable sentient beings may increase their roots of goodness.”
"Bhagavān!

I am now capable of serving as a messenger; out of compassion for the Great Tree Kinnara King, the assembly of Bodhisattvas, and the community of Śrāvakas, please come to Gandhamādana Mountain within seven days, out of pity for me."

At that time, the Kinnara King, knowing that the Buddha had granted his consent, was filled with such joy and exultation that it pervaded his entire body. Together with his wife, sons, daughters, and retinue, he performed various musical offerings for the Buddha, prostrated at the World-Honored One’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and departed from the assembly to return to Mount Gandhamādana.

At that time, the Great Kinnara King Druma, within the Fragrant Mountains, adorned his own garden where he dwelt as an offering to the Tathāgata; he embellished a wondrous ground five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with a floor of blue lapis lazuli interspersed with Jambūnada gold, where various precious colors shone upon one another.

At that time, hundreds of thousands of exquisite seats were spread upon the arena, interspersed with precious lotus flowers. Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial robes were laid out, and furthermore, for the Buddha-Tathāgata, a lion throne was prepared upon the arena, thirty-two *yojanas* in height, adorned with various jewels and surrounded by railings of diverse gems. Banners and canopies were unfurled, and many jeweled pillars were erected; immeasurable incense burners burned solid black aloeswood, while silk fabrics were spread above to catch the dust and dew. Banners, canopies, and silken streamers hung down on all sides, and celestial flowers were scattered everywhere. On the four sides of the throne, great jewel trees were fashioned, beautiful and variegated in color.
When many outsiders and his own retinue had all gathered together, he spoke these verses to instruct them:
“A Buddha appears in the world only once in a great while, Like the rare udumbara flower;
The Honored One among Men has now appeared in the world— One should respectfully honor and make offerings to him.”
Abandon arrogance, indolence, and deceit; likewise, leave behind stinginess, greed, and delusive illusions.
One should renounce all frivolous laughter and show proper reverence to the Teacher.
All manner of exquisite and pleasing flowers, the supreme flowers of the heavens and the blossoms of Mount Gandhamādana—
these all should be gathered together in one place to be offered to the Sage among Men.
All manner of exquisite and pleasing fragrances— Solid black aloeswood and sandalwood;
Within these Fragrant Mountains here, I shall burn them as an offering to the Supreme Being.
All the sounds of musical instruments and exquisite songs, which the kinnaras and others delight in;
each skillfully tuning these various musical instruments—these shall be used as offerings to the Sage, the Great Man.
Banners, pennants, precious parasols, and exquisite robes— soft, well-dyed, and pleasing to the celestial mind—
are spread out and set forth as offerings to the Tathāgata;
such things are difficult to encounter, difficult to obtain, and have no equal.
Having made offerings to the Buddha, they reach a state of excellence;
whether as Śakra or one of the Four Heavenly Kings, or as Brahmā or Maheśvara, they always become the honored kings among humans and devas!
Physical form, majestic power, and renown; Retinues, attendants, and precious treasures;
All teachings and instructions are fully enjoyed— Having made offerings to the Buddha, one attains these benefits.
The joys of the devas and the joys of humans, If one desires constant joy within birth and death,
And wishes to obtain eternal bliss and its requisites, One should make offerings to this supreme being.
If you wish to attain the vehicles of the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, Or to attain the most supreme and wondrous vehicle;
And if you wish to subdue the enemy Māra, You should perform offerings to the Dharma King!

At that time, after the Great Tree Kinnara King had thus instructed his retinue, he immediately gathered various flowers, garlands, unguents, and powdered incense, and prepared food of a hundred flavors. Then, before the King of Fragrant Mountains, he performed various musical instruments, sang verses of praise, and announced:
"The time has come."
“The Buddha is able to benefit and bestow peace and happiness; with a serene countenance, he smiles and speaks with gentle words.
Worthy of offerings from gods and humans as a sublime flower and a fine listener—O Sugata, the time has come; please come now.”
The One of Ten Powers has subdued all demonic forces; having vanquished the multitudes of others, he benefits the world.
Having severed all defilements, he is free from turbidity; the time has come—may the World-Honored One come to benefit the world.
Delighting in the practice of dhūta, free from defilement and attachment, those who have gathered supreme mindfulness and wisdom with firm resolve—
these superior persons constantly transcend the world, coming with a joyful heart to bring about benefit.
The light of the sun, moon, and jewels is eclipsed; The various lights of Śakra, Brahmā, and the devas are likewise obscured.
The light of the Muni brings joy to all; His sovereign radiance outshines every other light.
The songs of devas, nāgas, and kinnaras increase fetters and do not extinguish desire;
the Buddha’s voice, soft and like the Brahma-sound, can extinguish all fetters and bestow peace and happiness.
Worldly physicians wander throughout the ten directions, yet they cannot cure the disease of worldly afflictions;
the King of Physicians with Ten Powers proclaims the wondrous sound, extinguishing all fetters and granting peace and happiness.
Of great name and great power, peerless, with speech that is incomparable, unerring, and untainted;
who has subdued enmity, stilled enmity, and is free from all enmity—O World-Honored One, for the benefit of the world, we pray that you will come.
The donor who bestows the nectar of wisdom through generosity, the most excellent and venerable one who maintains and practices the precepts,
and he whose mind is refined by skillful patience— O beloved one, you have come here because of your mindfulness of me.
Well-endowed with the power of diligence and the corresponding dharmas, abiding in meditative concentration and possessing supernormal powers;
with wisdom that tames the mind and complete in the virtue of shame, you who bear the marks of a hundred merits—may you come at this time.
With great compassion and an impartial mind, Free from the faults of desire and craving, you leave no room for affliction;
Thoroughly knowing the Brahma-path and abiding in the Buddha-way, O World-Honored One who bestows happiness, we pray that you will come at this time.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the Great Tree Kinnara King had announced that the time had come, addressed the bhikṣus:
"Each of you take up your robes and bowls and accept the invitation for seven nights; appoint someone to guard the dwellings."
The Great Tree Kinnara King addressed him, saying, "The time has come.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva Diademed One thought to himself:

"I shall now manifest a great jeweled terrace, so that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, along with the assembly of bodhisattvas and the great śrāvaka saṃgha, may rest upon this jeweled terrace, seated upon lotus-throne seats adorned with jewels. I shall place them in my right palm and travel through the air to Mount Gandhamādana."

After the Bodhisattva Tiānguān (Cūḍāmaṇi) had formed this thought, he immediately entered into samādhi; by the power of that samādhi, he created a great precious terrace, ten yojanas in length, breadth, height, and depth, adorned with various exquisite colors and distinguished by four sides and four pillars.

At that time, hundreds of thousands of precious lotus seats emerged from within the jeweled platform; furthermore, for the World-Honored One, a precious lotus lion throne was spread out, seven fathoms in height.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tiānguān (Cūḍāmaṇi), having manifested a jeweled pavilion and a flower seat, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I pray that you, out of compassion for me, will take your place upon the lion throne within this jeweled pavilion, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. World-Honored One, I shall now place such a jeweled pavilion as this in my right palm and set it upon Mount Gandhamādana.”

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for the Bodhisattva Tiānguān, ascended the jeweled terrace and took his place upon the lion throne; the assembly of bodhisattvas and the community of śrāvakas then sat down in succession.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tiānguān (Cūḍāmaṇi) lifted the precious platform, placed it upon his right palm, and ascended into the void to proceed toward Mount Gandhamādana.

When the devas of the desire realm and the devas of the form realm beheld this miraculous transformation performed by the Bodhisattva Tiānguān, they leaped for joy with hearts full of wonder. To make offerings to the Buddha and the Bodhisattva Tiānguān, they took flowers, incense, garlands, ointments, powdered incense, and various musical instruments, and came to the precious platform. Remaining in the void, they made offerings to the Buddha and proceeded as far as Mount Gandhamādana.

At that time, the Great Kinnara King Druma saw from afar the Tathāgata coming through the air, seated within a precious pavilion. Having seen him, he, together with his retinue of eighty-four thousand kinnaras, took up fragrant flowers, garlands, powdered incense, and unguents, and performed eighty-four thousand kinds of music. Accompanied by pure and wondrous songs that harmonized well with the various instruments, they went forth to welcome the Tathāgata.

Having arrived, he and his retinue prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; after making offerings of the flowers, garlands, unguents, and powdered incense they had brought with them, they withdrew and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having known this, arrived at that place together with the bodhisattvas, the great assembly of śrāvakas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, and the great multitude; he proceeded to the abode of the Great Tree Kinnara King and sat upon the seat prepared for him within the adorned site of enlightenment.
At that time, the Great Kinnara King Druma addressed Śakra, Brahmā, the World Protectors, the various sons of gods, and the great virtuous ones, saying:
"Please come forward and take your seats; the food and drink prepared for the Tathāgata we shall enjoy together."

At that time, the Kinnara King, together with his wives, sons, daughters, and retinue, personally served the food with reverent devotion. It consisted of various sweet and delicious flavors, produced from the roots of virtue of the Bodhisattva; he made offerings to the Tathāgata, the Bodhisattvas, the Śrāvakas, and the entire assembly, so that all were fully satisfied.

Once they were fully satisfied, the Kinnara King, knowing that each had finished washing his bowl and rinsing his hands, sat down in succession before the Tathāgata together with his retinue, desiring to hear the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the sublime Dharma for the King of the Kinnaras and the great assembly, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them.
Then the World-Honored One spoke this sublime Dharma:
"King of the Kinnaras!..."
Bodhisattvas have thirty-two dharmas that purify the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
What are these thirty-two?
O King of Kinnaras!
The bodhisattva, never forgetting the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), practices giving as a guide.
He practices giving without praising the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
In all his actions, he practices giving with a mind free from malice or injury.
When there are those who come seeking, one practices giving with a mind free from malice.
Furthermore, regarding those who request [gifts], one practices giving while conceiving of them as fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Toward all those whom one approaches, one practices giving while conceiving of them as teachers and conceiving of them as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
They practice giving by abandoning the internal fetter of stinginess;
they practice giving with joy and exultation, free from greed and attachment;
they practice giving by extending their hands with integrity and noble generosity, without expectation of reward.
One practices giving by generating a superior mind and not a lowly mind;
one practices giving without being reborn in evil realms;
and one practices giving without hoping for karmic rewards or harboring any expectations.
One practices giving with the desire for the Buddha-dharma;
one practices giving with a mind free from affliction and feverish distress;
and one practices giving with the gathering [of beings] as the primary aim.
I shall practice giving in order to instruct and transform all sentient beings.
I shall practice giving in order to protect the Dharma.
I shall practice giving in accordance with the teachings of the Tathāgata.
I should practice giving as an ally in the subduing of Māra;
I should practice giving for the sake of perfectly awakening to Bodhi;
I should practice giving as the deed of a true hero.
"I should practice giving while remaining free from the realm of hungry ghosts and the evil paths.
I should practice giving by cultivating and accumulating a mind of equanimity.
I should practice giving so as to acquire great wealth and fiefs, thereby benefiting others."
I should practice giving while practicing the dharma of harmony and respect.
I should practice giving without being separated from the acquisition of spiritual friends.
I should practice giving with eyes free from anger or malice toward all sentient beings.
"I should practice giving by directing the roots of goodness from my own giving toward the Unsurpassed Way.
I should learn to practice giving by emulating the renunciation of other bodhisattvas."
"I ought to practice giving in order to adorn myself with the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
I ought to practice giving in order to purify the Buddha-fields,
O King of Kinnaras!"
These are the thirty-two dharmas for purifying the *dānapāramitā* of a bodhisattva.
"Kinnara King! Furthermore, there are thirty-two dharmas for purifying the *śīlapāramitā* of a bodhisattva."
Thoroughly purifying one’s own body is called precept, for it purifies greed, hatred, and delusion;
thoroughly purifying one’s own speech is called precept, for it does not deceive oneself or the Buddhas and devas, being free from the characteristic of falsehood;
thoroughly purifying one’s own mind is called precept, for it is detached from ignorance, greed, hatred, and false views.
Purifying the ten wholesome courses of action is called morality, for it leads to birth among humans and devas.
Not forgetting the bodhicitta is called morality, for one does not crave other vehicles.
Purity of intention is called precept, for it abandons illusion and falsehood.
Praising the noble and holy ones is called precept, for it diligently gathers in those who are not yet noble.
Taking loving-kindness as the foremost is called precept, for the mind is impartial toward all sentient beings.
Cultivating the mind of great compassion is called precept, because it leads toward the transformation and edification of all sentient beings.
Thoroughly and correctly training in the studies is called precept, because it is ultimately without deficiency.
That which is embraced by shame and remorse is called morality, because of the fear of the evil realms.
That which is without breach or leakage is called morality, because it is not abandoned midway.
That which is without flaw is called morality, because it is the ultimate purity of the white dharmas.
Mastery over oneself is called morality, for it leads to other Buddha-fields.
Being honored and noble is called morality, for it is praised by the wise.
That which is able to transcend and surpass [all faults] is called morality (*śīla*), because it brings one away from the evil realms.
That which is well-established and settled is called morality, because it is fully endowed with all peace and happiness.
That which is praised by all Buddhas is called precept, for it is the Buddha-precept.
Not being self-indulgent or lax is called precept, for it is firm and solid in rescuing and uplifting those in the world.
Not exalting oneself and not disparaging others is called precept, because of its excellence in relinquishment.
Cultivating relinquishment is called precept, because of being free from all afflictions.
One's own practice is called precept, because it consists of all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Bringing forth joy is called precept, because it is free from craving and greed.
Skillfully gathering others is called morality, because it accords with what has been taught.
Subduing oneself and leaving the household life is called morality, because it relinquishes all bonds of domestic attachment.
Firmly desiring to practice is called morality, because of the desire for the Dharma.
Resolutely possessing few desires and being content is called morality, because of relying on the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
Delighting in the practice of dhūta is called precept, because it seeks to abandon all unwholesome dharmas.
Being in accord with non-attachment is called precept, because it contemplates the non-existence of sentient beings.
To follow and not oppose is called precept, because it accords with the Dharma of conditions.
To be free from all views is called precept, because it is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. Kinnara King!
These are the thirty-two dharmas by which a bodhisattva purifies the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
"Kinnara King! Furthermore, there are thirty-two dharmas by which a bodhisattva purifies the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā)."
What are these thirty-two?
Not being firmly attached to the body is called knowing patience.
Not dwelling on the life-span is called knowing patience.
A mind free from malice is called knowing patience;
enduring harsh words is called knowing patience;
feeling compassion for those who are inferior is called knowing patience.
Not disparaging those who have not yet studied is called knowing patience.
Possessing great power and influence, one does not inflict suffering or harshness upon others; this is called knowing patience.
Even when one's limbs and joints are severed one by one, one does not give rise to anger; this is called knowing patience.
To be free from harshness and coarseness is called knowing patience;
to give rise to neither anger nor malice is called knowing patience;
to refrain from not speaking with others is called knowing patience.
To have such an intention is called knowing patience;
for the mind to be free from turbidity is called knowing patience;
for the mind to be without agitation is called knowing patience.
Protecting the minds of others is called knowing patience.
Benefiting them with material wealth is called knowing patience.
Realizing great compassion is called knowing patience.
To eliminate arrogance is called knowing patience.
To humble oneself before all sentient beings is called knowing patience.
Not to increase one's blazing passion is called knowing patience.
Delighting in tranquility is called knowing patience;
being secluded, leisurely, and unconditioned is called knowing patience;
observing one's own faults is called knowing patience.
Not seeing the faults of others when they have deficiencies is called knowing patience.
Possessing the wealth of the Dharma is called knowing patience.
Having the wealth of faith is called knowing patience.
To have no feverish affliction in the mind is called knowing patience.
To have peace and happiness in one's thoughts is called knowing patience.
To first inquire with courtesy and to have no angry countenance is called knowing patience.
To accord with the profound Dharma is called the knowledge of patience.
To accord with the three gates of liberation is called the knowledge of patience.
To understand non-arising and non-origination is called the knowledge of patience regarding the endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
“Kinnara King!
These are the thirty-two dharmas of the bodhisattva’s perfection of pure patience. Kinnara King!”
Furthermore, there are thirty-two dharmas that purify the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
What are these thirty-two?
O King of Kinnaras!
The Bodhisattva practices the perfection of vigor by not severing the lineage of the Buddhas;
practices the perfection of vigor by not severing the lineage of the Saṅgha;
and practices the perfection of vigor by undergoing immeasurable births and deaths.
One practices the perfection of vigor by accumulating immeasurable roots of goodness;
one practices the perfection of vigor by making offerings to and serving immeasurable Buddhas;
and one practices the perfection of vigor for the sake of upholding immeasurable learning.
One practices the perfection of vigor for the sake of teaching and guiding immeasurable sentient beings;
one practices the perfection of vigor desiring to gladden all sentient beings with sublime speech.
One practices the perfection of vigor in order to cause all sentient beings to go against the current.
One practices the perfection of vigor by considering what is appropriate for all sentient beings.
One practices the perfection of vigor by relinquishing all that one possesses.
The perfection of vigor practiced by guarding all precepts without violation or deficiency;
the perfection of vigor practiced through the power of patience and gentleness toward all, without anger;
and the perfection of vigor practiced by transcending all conditioned activities.
One practices the perfection of vigor because one desires to give rise to all meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis;
one practices the perfection of vigor because one desires to fulfill immeasurable wisdom;
and one practices the perfection of vigor because one desires to adorn one's own buddha-field with all the adornments found in all the buddha-fields of all the Buddhas.
One practices the perfection of vigor because of possessing great power and firmness that transcends to the other shore;
one practices the perfection of vigor because of subduing all the realms of Māra;
one practices the perfection of vigor because of subduing all the treatises of non-Buddhist paths.
One practices the perfection of vigor because of possessing the ten powers and the qualities of fearlessness of a Buddha;
one practices the perfection of vigor because of adorning the body, speech, and mind;
and one practices the perfection of vigor because of being able to accomplish all tasks without rest.
One practices the perfection of vigor because the mind is free from cowardice;
one practices the perfection of vigor because the mind is courageous and robust;
one practices the perfection of vigor because it does not dwell together with any afflictions or fetters.
One practices the perfection of vigor in order to subdue all afflictions;
one practices the perfection of vigor in order to extinguish all fetters;
one practices the perfection of vigor in order to cross over the floods.
One practices the perfection of vigor in order to liberate those not yet liberated, to bring peace to those not yet at peace, and to deliver those not yet delivered.
One practices the perfection of vigor in order to accumulate the hundredfold merits that adorn the marks of a Great Man.
One practices the perfection of vigor in order to protect the true Dharma of all Buddhas.
One practices the perfection of vigor in order to reach all Buddha-fields through supernormal powers to make offerings to, prostrate before, circumambulate clockwise, and revere all Buddhas.
This diligence arises from tranquility; it abides in the tranquility of body and mind, without exiting or entering, without rising or falling, and is subsumed within the unborn and the unarisen.
"Kinnara King!
These are the thirty-two dharmas by which a bodhisattva purifies the perfection of vigor. Kinnara King!"
Furthermore, there are thirty-two dharmas by which a bodhisattva purifies the dhyāna-pāramitā.
What are these thirty-two dharmas? They are as follows:
namely, purity of mindfulness.
Purity of wisdom,
purity of diligence,
and purity of shame.
Purity of firmness;
purity of the essential nature of the mind;
and purity of not forgetting the bodhicitta.
The faculty of merit is pure;
that which is without dependence is pure;
the notions of "I" and "mine" are pure.
The purity of arising supernormal powers;
the purity of bodily tranquility;
the purity of cultivating and refining the mind.
Purity of inner tranquility;
purity of external deportment;
and purity of severing all attachments to views.
The purity of contemplating the absence of self, the absence of sentient beings, the absence of persons, the absence of life-span, and the absence of individuals;
the purity of not abiding in the three realms;
and the purity of the manifestation of the factors conducive to enlightenment.
The purity of compassionately observing sentient beings;
the purity of removing the cognitive obscurations;
and the purity of transcendent wisdom.
The purity of not contradicting cause and effect;
the purity of the certainty of dharma-patience;
and the purity of practicing the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.
Purity of the transformation of skillful means;
purity of the inclusion of skillful means;
purity of proximity to the site of enlightenment.
They do not aspire for the purity of the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
they fulfill the purity of the untainted (anāsrava);
and with an undistracted mind, they attain the purity of the Buddha-concentration (buddha-samādhi).
One should explain the purification of the minds of sentient beings as appropriate. Kinnara King!
These are the thirty-two dharmas for the purification of the bodhisattva’s dhyāna-pāramitā.
“Kinnara King! Furthermore, there are thirty-two dharmas by which a bodhisattva purifies the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
What are these thirty-two?
They seek to accumulate extensive learning without ever feeling weary or satisfied; they skillfully contemplate and discern all phenomena, awakening to them through their own wisdom.
They skillfully discern the aggregates (*skandhas*) and skillfully discern the elements (*dhātus*), because they are intent upon the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
He is skilled in the sense bases (*āyatana*) because he knows their differentiation;
he is skilled in conditioned phenomena (*dharmas*) because he knows their causal abiding;
he is skilled in the truths (*satya*) because he knows their cessation through realization.
One knows the state of correctness because one does not enter the state of correctness;
one observes non-arising because arising is of one's own mind;
one knows that all phenomena are unborn because the primordial limit is pure.
They know that all sentient beings are without self, because they are free from inverted views.
They know that all phenomena are one and the same phenomenon, because their original limit is free from desire.
They know that all worlds are one world, because they are identical to empty space.
They know that all Buddhas are one and the same Buddha, for they have entered the inconceivable Dharma-realm.
They skillfully discern all chapters and phrases, for they are proficient in language and letters.
They possess unimpeded eloquence to extensively expound the Dharma in order to gladden all sentient beings;
they know dhāraṇīs so as to never forget them;
and they know the activities of all māras in order to transform those māras toward bodhi.
One contemplates and knows that all phenomena abide in conceptual discrimination like illusions, because they possess distinctions.
One understands and realizes that all phenomena are like lightning, the moon in water, a dream, a shadow, and an echo, because all phenomena are ultimately unestablished.
They realize the nature of the minds of all sentient beings, for it is inherently pure from the beginning.
They skillfully discern and contemplate saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, for they have skillfully studied expedient means.
They skillfully know and understand emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, for they manifest the gates of liberation.
One knows that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is quiescent, because they are fundamentally free from bondage and obstruction.
One knows that all phenomena are free from hindrances and attain clarity, because they destroy the darkness of ignorance.
He skillfully understands wisdom and bestows the light of insight in order to preach the Dharma for the liberation of all sentient beings;
he knows all phenomena because they have neither coming nor going.
Because they know the actions performed and do not contradict them;
because they know how to manifest [the truth] to sentient beings by demonstrating birth and death;
and because they have attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)—namely, the analytical knowledge of meaning, phenomena, language, and eloquence.
What has been spoken is without error; there is no phenomenon that is not empty.
One is personally tranquil, disciplined, and attains true knowledge of nirvāṇa; through wisdom, one directs oneself toward the wisdom of all Buddhas.
He guards the city of the Dharma, upholds all dharmas, attains the stage of receiving the prediction, and brings his tasks to completion.
He dwells on the stage of the non-regressive Bodhisattva.
O King of Kinnaras!
These are the thirty-two dharmas by which a bodhisattva purifies the perfection of wisdom.
"Kinnara King! Furthermore, there are thirty-two dharmas by which a bodhisattva purifies the perfection of skillful means."
What are these thirty-two? They are:
observing that sentient beings themselves are free from all evils;
possessing immeasurable merit without ceasing; and never resting even when one possesses only a small amount of merit.
To transform sentient beings, he practices giving without seeking fields of merit;
toward all sentient beings, he conceives the thought that they are fields of merit and does not hope for karmic retribution.
To teach those who are inferior, he manifests as one who is inferior.
They teach all sentient beings to guard their verbal karma;
they manifest in the form of women to transform young men,
and manifest as youths to transform young girls.
He manifests all forms without contradicting sentient beings.
Though he himself is free from arrogance and self-indulgence, he manifests arrogance and self-indulgence in order to transform those sentient beings who are arrogant and self-indulgent.
He displays madness and confusion, preaching the Dharma according to what sentient beings understand.

Even if one has observed the precepts for a hundred years for the sake of converting a single person, one should relinquish all such observances and every possession of pleasure and entertainment, sharing them instead to gather that person and lead them into the Dharma.
While personally abiding in the dhūta ascetic practices, he manifests the fear of being unable to subsist for the sake of those sentient beings who fear such insecurity.
He demonstrates the practice of renunciation within all the systems of external paths, yet never disparages the Buddha-dharma.
He manifests as a courtesan, or if in a royal palace, manifests as the body of a sublime woman, in order to transform sentient beings who are stingy and attached to sensual desire.

Among great assemblies and places where many people gather, he manifests various arts and skills; whether manifesting the flute, the pipe, the lute, the zither, the drum, or the conch, he is always the foremost.

Thereupon, amidst the assembly, they sang, danced, played, and laughed; all produced the sounds of the Dharma and displayed various arts and skills, manifesting whatever was pleasing to the various sentient beings for the sake of their conversion and instruction.
He manifests supernatural powers to bestow wealth upon sentient beings and only then preaches the Dharma.
To those who have lost their wealth, he manifests a treasure trove and only then preaches the Dharma.
For those sentient beings oppressed by the arrows of sorrow, he manifests what is appropriate for each and only then preaches the Dharma.

If there are elders, householders, minor kings, or women of the inner palace who grieve over having no offspring, [the Bodhisattva], desiring to transform and guide them and cause them joy, manifests as their son.

Among a great multitude, he acts as their leader; taking the crowd to a vast wilderness where provisions are exhausted and nothing can be found, he uses his supernormal powers to manifest food and drink so that they are fully satisfied, and then teaches them the Dharma as appropriate, causing them not to regress from the unsurpassed path.

If there are sentient beings who have been blind since birth and follow one another in groups—whether one, two, three, or four, up to eleven, a hundred, a thousand, two thousand, or even ten thousand—he manifests before that multitude as a blind man and as one in extreme poverty. He begs from outsiders to provide for those blind ones, causing them to regain their sight and perceive all forms; he then preaches the Dharma according to their needs, enabling them not to regress from the unsurpassed path.

Furthermore, if there are many thousands of sentient beings who have committed various transgressions and are imprisoned by the king, the Bodhisattva, in order to liberate these beings from their confinement in prison, manifests as a criminal and enters therein together with them. By means of his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he completely removes their shackles and fetters, provides them with clothing, and supplies them with sufficient food and drink. He then teaches them the Dharma so that they do not regress from the unsurpassed path.

If there are sentient beings who have committed an offense for which they ought to die, [the Buddha], for the sake of teaching and transforming them, manifests a transformation person to take the place of that offender so that their life may be preserved and they are freed from anxiety. He consoles and gladdens them, then preaches the Dharma for them, whereby they become firmly established in the unsurpassed, right path.

If there are sentient beings who contend over wealth and profit, slaves, livestock, houses, or fields, striking one another and engaging in disputes and litigation, [the Bodhisattva], through the power of skillful means, manifests great treasures to recompense these people and cause them to reach a reconciliation; thereafter, he teaches the Dharma so that they may abide in the practice of bodhi.

Through skillful means, bodhisattvas manifest bodies that are deaf, blind, mute, or speech-impaired, and assume forms that are crippled or ugly; they relinquish their own exquisite forms to appear like those beings for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Or again, they may manifest as teachers of non-Buddhist paths, remaining at a distance while praising the Triple Gem, so as to ensure the continuity of the Buddha-seed.
Through skillful means, Bodhisattvas relinquish their various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and take birth in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) in order to transform sentient beings.

Or again, they manifest as those beyond training (aśaikṣa), who, aspiring for the attainment of bliss, demonstrate the entry into nirvāṇa while redoubling their diligent effort in cultivating all dharmic practices.

Bodhisattvas of skillful means manifest the practice of cultivation, attain the stage of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma), and appear to enter nirvāṇa, yet they have only just begun to cultivate the most sublime and wondrous conduct.
A Bodhisattva of skillful means manifests the form of a Tathāgata before those who have not yet attained the stage of certainty and desire nirvāṇa, in order to cause such persons to abide in bodhi.
"Kinnara King!
These are the thirty-two dharmas by which a bodhisattva fulfills the perfection of skillful means.

When these perfections were thus spoken, among the retinue of the Great Tree Kinnara King, nine hundred and sixty thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Among the assembly of the Tathāgata, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti);
the Kinnara King Mahādruma attained the Samādhi of the Lamp of Wisdom.
At that time, the Kinnara King Mahādruma!

Having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, which instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him, he was filled with joy and exultation, attaining what he had never experienced before. He offered priceless garments to the World-Honored One; the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas each offered their own robes, and he dedicated his own park and everything contained within it as an offering to the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Great Kinnara King Mahādruma had eight thousand sons, who adorned eight thousand exquisite parasols with various precious flowers and offered them to the Tathāgata.

While the parasols were being offered, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, all the precious parasols were made to merge into a single canopy in mid-air, covering an area of one hundred *yojanas*.

At that time, the eight thousand sons of the Kinnara King, beholding the Buddha’s supernatural power, leaped for joy with unprecedented delight; with focused minds and resolute intent, they gave rise to the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, becoming firm and non-retrogressive.
Having each resolved their minds [on enlightenment], they addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you grant us the dharmas that assist awakening; having heard them, we shall practice them.”
The Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra, Scroll Two.
The Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra, Scroll Three.
Translated by Kumārajīva, Tripiṭaka Master of Kucha during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the inclinations and desires in the hearts of the sons of the Kinnara King,
ascended into the air to a height of seven tala trees and emitted a great radiance.

This light shone everywhere throughout this trichiliocosm; all the musical instruments of the various devas in the desire realm, as well as those of the gandharvas, kinnaras, and others, resounded with exquisite sounds spontaneously, without being struck.
All the trees within King Gandhamādana also produced subtle and wondrous musical sounds.
At that time, the World-Honored One again emitted immeasurable billions of rays of light from each of the pores on his body;
at the tip of each ray of light was a lotus flower, and within each flower sat a bodhisattva, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, seated upon the flower pedestal.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the World-Honored One caused the musical instruments to perform verses of wisdom that inquired about all doubts. He then caused all the bodhisattvas upon the flower pedestals to answer those questions with individual verses:
"How is it that one gives rise to The unsurpassed mind of awakening?
How does one never forget this mind Until the realization of enlightenment?"
Accomplishing single-minded devotion for the sake of all sentient beings;
Arising the adornment of great compassion, never forgetting the bodhicitta.
What is their resolve? How should they practice?
Regarding the great compassionate mind that has been described: how does it arise?
When one’s intention is free from flattery and deceit, and one’s practice is without hypocrisy;
when one abides in the nirvāṇa of sentient beings—such is that great compassion!
How does one practice giving so that, having given, the mind remains free from feverish distress;
and without hoping for a reward, how does one dedicate the merit toward enlightenment?
Giving up everything that can be given, one feels no regret after having given.
Advancing toward the path to enlightenment, one does not look for karmic reward.
How can one abide in the precepts without giving rise to pride regarding those precepts?
Saving those who have violated the prohibitions—what Great Vehicle could be superior to this?
Precepts are the bodhicitta; being empty and non-arising, do not give rise to pride.
Give rise to the mind of great compassion to rescue those who violate the prohibitions.
How can one endure sentient beings’ reviling and scolding?
The mind never gives rise to anger, but instead increases joy all the more.
I am a physician for sentient beings, healing their manifold ailments;
even after hearing harsh words, I do not give rise to resentment.
How does one advance in practice? How does one cultivate and accumulate practice?
How does the mind remain untiring while cultivating the conduct of enlightenment?
One exerts diligence to protect sentient beings and constantly strives to protect the Dharma.
With all roots of goodness fully satisfied, their minds know no weariness.
How do they cultivate right mindfulness so as to advance with courageous vigor?
How do they cultivate meditative concentration so that the mind does not scatter?
Without wandering thoughts, with wisdom free from deceit and hypocrisy, practicing dhyāna through skillful means, his mind does not scatter.
How does one attain wisdom? How does one see with uprightness?
How does one make a firm resolve? How does one discern phenomena?
By cultivating learning, wisdom increases; by practicing what one has learned, the mind becomes upright.
Resolutely practicing the gift of Dharma, one cultivates according to the meaning.
How does one seek to hear? How does one become possessed of much learning?
How does one hear according to what was taught? And how does a Great Being depart?
By listening with reverence and by associating with those who possess much learning.
They speak not for the sake of wealth or profit; such is the way the Great Beings depart.
How do they practice loving-kindness? How do they practice great compassion?
How do they fully accomplish joy and equanimity? And how do they abide in the Brahma-path?
With a mind of loving-kindness that is entirely impartial, And great compassion free from weariness;
Rejoicing is what is called "joy," Which enables one to reach the Brahma-path.
How may one come to see the Buddha, And having seen him, give rise to faith?
How does one hear the Dharma? How does one eliminate doubt?
By practicing mindfulness of the Buddha, one beholds the World’s Teacher;
with faith fully perfected, having heard the Dharma, one is free from doubt.
What is the adornment of merit? What is the adornment of wisdom?
If there are concentration and insight, how do they constitute an adornment?
One never tires of adorning merit; through study, one adorns wisdom.
The stillness of the mind is called concentration; knowing phenomena is called wisdom.
What is that sphere of practice? What are the characteristics of dwelling therein?
What is that sphere of practice like? How does one cultivate it?
He practices in the sphere of the emptiness of phenomena, having abandoned these words of the other shore;
he practices by abiding in the four dhyānas, cultivating the path to liberate sentient beings.
What constitutes the work of Māra, and what is the Buddha’s true work?
By performing what kind of karma does one obtain the protection of bodhi?
The Lesser Vehicle constitutes the work of Māra, while the Mahāyāna is the supreme path;
by abandoning all evil, one obtains the protection of bodhi.
How does one associate with a virtuous friend? What are the characteristics of an evil friend?
How does one proceed with equanimity? How does one abandon false views?
If one praises the path to enlightenment, one should draw near to such a person as a virtuous friend.
The bodhicitta is perfectly pure; one abandons evil associates.
Having understood all karmic actions, one practices with upright view;
abandoning association with the heterodox, one does not lose right view.
How does one protect the True Dharma and transform sentient beings?
What are those skillful means by which one can attain Bodhi?
By diligently protecting the True Dharma and employing skillful means, one is able to transform others.
Having abandoned the flow of the two extremes, one is able to attain supreme enlightenment.
How does one perform the work of wisdom? How does one perform agreeable deeds?
How does one swiftly receive the teachings? And how does one always respectfully circumambulate to the right?
Non-contention is the work of wisdom; one does not give rise to disputes or litigation.
With gentle and virtuous speech, one pays respect and circumambulates to the right.
What are the characteristics of the Path? And what constitutes that which is not the Path?
How can one establish those beings who dwell upon paths inconceivable?
The Six Perfections are the true path; the Lesser Vehicle is not the path.
Having mastered the wisdom of skillful means, one causes sentient beings to abide upon the path.
How does one attain great wealth? How does one obtain great benefit?
Where is the treasure-trove located? How does one fulfill sentient beings?
The seven riches constitute great wealth; tranquility constitutes great benefit.
A treasury of dhāraṇīs, with eloquent discourse made full.
Who were his parents? What was the appearance of his kinsmen?
What was the appearance of his attendants? How did that one of wisdom adorn himself?
Wisdom is the mother who carries one across to the further shore; the factors conducive to enlightenment are the kinsmen;
and all roots of goodness are the attendants—these adorn the wise one.
Having realized the selflessness of phenomena, their heart of loving-kindness pervades the world.
What is the meaning of "non-self" and "loving-kindness"?
If one understands emptiness, one naturally realizes non-self;
this is the supreme loving-kindness, for one knows emptiness in this very life.
The future has no coming; such is the nature of all conditioned phenomena!
Such too is the retribution of karma!
How, then, can there be birth?
In the ultimate sense, there is no "is," nor is there any one who goes;
yet entering the path of worldly convention, one speaks of karma and its retribution.
If it be emptiness, signlessness, and the liberation of wishlessness;
The single characteristic is identical to the absence of characteristics; how then is the Path produced?
Emptiness is itself the absence of characteristics, and it is through this absence of characteristics that it is attained.
The single characteristic and the single meaning are thus called the gates of liberation.
How does one contemplate emptiness? How does one contemplate sentient beings?
From whence do emptiness and sentient beings arise?
Through wisdom one contemplates emptiness; through skillful means one contemplates sentient beings.
Through great compassion, one teaches and transforms others, directing them toward nirvāṇa.
There is no birth and no arising; all phenomena are thus!
How can various conditioned formations arise? One should understand this meaning.
Non-arising and non-ceasing are the sphere of activity of wisdom;
born from the power of vows, this is established through skillful means.
How does one receive the prediction of enlightenment? How does one become irreversible?
What is the object of patience? How does one attain certainty?
Abiding in equality, one receives the prophecy; within the dharmadhātu, one is non-retrogressive.
Non-arising is the condition for patience; by knowing the Dharma, one attains certainty.
What is the locus of the site of enlightenment? What are the characteristics of bodhi?
Who is named Tathāgata? How does a Buddha attain clarity?
Space is called the site of enlightenment; bodhi has the characteristic of space.
"Not relying on body or mind—suchness is called the Tathāgata!

At that time, having heard this teaching, the sons of the Great Tree Kiṃnara King attained the patience of compliance with the Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*). Each offered their own jeweled necklaces to the Tathāgata and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, we have today been able to hear this most profound Dharma.
How rare it is, World-Honored One!

You were able to cause verses to be spoken within the sounds of musical instruments to inquire about doubts, and caused the image of a Bodhisattva to answer those questions, thereby severing all the doubts of the great assembly; having heard this, we have attained the great light of the Dharma."
“World-Honored One!
By whom is this upheld?
At that time, the Buddha replied:
“O worthy sirs!
You should know that all this is through the power of the Tathāgata; the Buddha’s power is thus inconceivable.
At that time, the prince Mahādruma Kinnara addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that all sentient beings may likewise attain such power.

At that time, the Great Kinnara King Druma, together with his queen and eighty-four thousand court ladies, each holding a string of pearls in their hands, went to where the World-Honored One was. Upon arrival, they bowed their heads to the Buddha’s feet in reverent salutation and each scattered the pearl strings as an offering over the Buddha.

At the moment they were dispersed, through the supernatural power of the Buddha, eighty-four thousand great pearl platforms manifested in mid-air. Adorned with four pillars on each side, their decorations were distinct and clear; within each jeweled platform was a seat, along with various treasures, necklaces, and hundreds of thousands of celestial garments. Upon each of these seats sat a Tathāgata in the full lotus posture, self-adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.

At that time, the Kinnara King and his eighty-four thousand queens, beholding the Buddha’s supernatural power, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness at such an unprecedented occurrence. With profound resolve, they all brought forth the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Having thus resolved their minds, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; all together with one voice, they praised and extolled the Tathāgata in verse:
"Most supreme and unsurpassed, worthy of offerings, The benefit you bring is inconceivable;
Well-trained in the Dharma of benefit and discipline, I now prostrate to the Supreme Person."
Free from greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as deceit and hypocrisy; possessing a fearless voice that is free from the habitual tendencies of afflictions;
revealing the Dharma from the great treasury of jewels—I bow my head and pay homage to the Honored One who has transcended desire.
The five eyes are pure and free from defilement; you are skillfully able to subdue all enemies and adversaries.
Unstained by the three realms of existence like a lotus flower, I prostrate to you who have reached the further shore.
Able to bestow upon the world the eye of clear wisdom, Able to eclipse the radiance of the sun and moon;
Born from the lineage of the Cakravartin Sage-Kings, I pay homage to you who uphold the mark of the wheel.
His mind is ever unstained by any forms; the Guide is our refuge and our protection.
There is none equal to the Honored One, much less any superior; I prostrate to him who proclaims with wondrous voice.
Equanimous toward gain and loss, you fully understand all worldly phenomena;
you liberate those fallen into the net of craving—to the World-Honored One, the Guide, I pay homage.
Constantly taming the mind and abiding in meditative concentration, Burning away all fetters and dwelling throughout the ten directions;
Expounding the gift of Dharma rather than the gift of food— To this unsurpassed field of merit, I prostrate with my head.
Your speech is subtle and endowed with the marks and signs; you have abandoned and distanced yourself from the left-hand paths.
Your voice is soft like the sound of thunder; I prostrate to you who have transcended the three realms.
The Honored Among Men has already transcended the affliction of burning heat; with supernormal powers, he travels to immeasurable lands.
Having fashioned a sturdy vessel to ferry the world across, I prostrate and pay homage to the Tathāgata!
The World-Honored One proclaims faith and diligence, Delivering the world from all fetters and obstructions;
To the sixfold path of practice of the śrāvakas, Which transcends the six realms of existence, I bow my head in praise.
I now bow my head to the one with the color of a golden mountain; I bow my head to the one whose faculties are tamed and stilled in concentration.
I now bow my head to the one with a face like the full moon; I bow my head to the supreme among men, whose virtues are served by all.
Subduing all the fetters of sentient beings, Crossing over the river of the four floods so difficult to traverse;
We now take refuge in this one, The World-Honored One who tames the faculties—to you we pay homage.
In former lives, the Honored One practiced great generosity; He gave with a joyful heart to those who came begging.
Giving away even his most cherished and beloved treasures to others— I pay homage to the heroic Dānaśūra, who severed [attachment] well.
Beholding sentient beings intoxicated by ignorance and pride, he thoroughly understands the causes they have created;
having attained the supreme and unsurpassed path, the Honored One skillfully guides them to settle in this state.
The nature of the aggregates and elements is eternally empty and still; all fetters are without reality, existing only as deceptive illusions.
The Teacher has severed all worldly doubts and regrets; I pay homage to the World-Honored One who speaks at the proper time.
Abiding eternally in the true dharmas and all samādhis, you have attained mastery over all phenomena and reached the further shore;
with wisdom as your supreme guide, I prostrate to you, the Great Caravan Leader.
Free from illusion, falsehood, and all deceptions, he of great power subdues the hosts of Māra;
this wise and virtuous person, supreme among men, is like a mighty wind that meets no obstruction.
Having exhausted the depths of all outflows and reached the further shore, the precious treasury of the Honored One among Men is inexhaustible;
like the sands of the Ganges are the Tathāgatas whom you constantly made offerings to during your past practices.
Having attained immovability within the world, And having reached the further shore, free from the afflictions of craving;
Drawing near to all Buddhas and dwelling in the auspicious state— Therefore, I pay homage to the Supreme among Men.
Having cast off the terrors of birth, old age, sickness, and death, he recalls his billions of past lives;
the vast net of craving is most fearsome, yet the light of the sun of wisdom causes it to wither away.
The Teacher, the Solitary Realizer, has awakened to all phenomena; his hands and feet bear the auspicious mark of wheels.
Auspiciously, I offer soft grass; auspiciously, I prostrate my head to the World-Honored One.
Mastery of the transcendent dhāraṇī, Constantly bestowing the gift of Dharma rather than material wealth;
O Benevolent Honored One who beats the great Dharma drum, To you, the Dharma King, the World-Honored One, I pay homage and praise.
Born from the lineage of the Śākya kings, With senses ever tranquil and mind likewise serene;
The Teacher of the three realms is eternally extinguished— I pay homage to you whose mind is thus peaceful.
The Māra King arrived, brandishing a sharp sword, along with his hosts of demons beneath the King of Trees;
yet he could not cause a single hair of the Honored One to stand on end. Unmoving like a mountain, [the Bodhisattva] bowed his head in praise.
The Honored One among Men has reached the further shore of diligence; for the sake of all sentient beings, he bears and endures suffering.
Having exhausted birth and death, he no longer undergoes existence; I praise and pay homage to the World-Honored One who teaches patience.
Having attained great power, you are unshakable; You dwell well in the state of fearlessness regarding what is possible and impossible;
You establish immeasurable multitudes in awakening— To the World-Honored One, so well-established, I pay homage with praise.
Knowing that all conditioned things are not firm, you renounced your kin and went forth into homelessness;
knowing that the Triple Existence is supreme and unsurpassed, I pay homage to you, the Wise One who has reached the further shore.
Sentient beings suffer in affliction without protection; you satisfy them with the Dharma of the Triple Gem.
You establish them upon the path that is free from difficulty; I prostrate my head to the World-Honored One, the true Savior.
The Honored One cultivates the power of wisdom and knows all faculties; he has shattered the hosts of Māra’s evil armies.
His spoken voice is most supreme and wondrous; I pay homage to him who has well cultivated all faculties.
The root of hearing the true Dharma is aspiration; through that aspiration, one further aspires for enlightenment.
You provide impartial and universal shelter, making no distinction between kin and stranger. To you, the true protector of the world, I pay homage.
The Sugata, having personally awakened to all phenomena, Turns the unsurpassed, holy wheel of Dharma himself;
Knowing that the characteristics of all conditioned things are like a dream, He causes all sentient beings to recognize reality.
At that time, after the consorts of the Great Tree Kinnara King had praised the Buddha with verses, they addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We have all resolved to attain the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment; we shall never achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in these female bodies.”
Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will preach the Dharma for us as is appropriate, so that we may cast off our female bodies and obtain male bodies, swiftly attaining the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the queens and ladies of the Kinnara King: "Sisters!
Listen attentively and reflect well upon this; I shall expound how one may cast off the female body and become a male body, swiftly attaining the unsurpassed, true, and correct path."
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall listen with reverence.
The Buddha said:
"Sisters! If women accomplish one practice, they shall cast off their female forms and obtain male bodies, and quickly attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
What is this one?
It is the bodhicitta.
The mind of omniscience is identical to this single mind; it is the most supreme mind within the entire triple world, never forgetting the adornments of all roots of goodness.
"Sisters!
This is the one dharma that, when accomplished by a woman, causes her to cast off the female body and obtain a male body, swiftly attaining the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
"Furthermore, sisters!
If women accomplish two dharmas, they will cast off the female body and obtain a male body, swiftly attaining the unsurpassed, true, and correct path."
What are the two? They are:
attending upon the Buddha rather than other deities, and being free from wrong views.
These are the two.
She shall cast off her female body and swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
"Furthermore, sisters,
if a woman accomplishes three dharmas, she shall cast off her female body and become a man."
What are the three?
They are the precept of body, the precept of speech, and the precept of mind.
These are the three.
"Furthermore, sisters!
If women accomplish four dharmas, they will transform their female bodies and become men.
What are these four?
That is to say, one practices giving with a mind free from conditioned constructs;
one cultivates and maintains ethical discipline without hypocrisy;
and one approaches the noble ones with a sense of reverence.
To listen to and receive the true Dharma— this is the fourth.
"Furthermore, sisters!
If a woman accomplishes five qualities, she will transform her female body and become a man.
What are these five? They are:
loving the Dharma and delighting in the Dharma.
Desiring the Dharma and listening to the Dharma,
once he has heard it, he observes with right mindfulness and comes to feel revulsion for the female body.
She always delights in desiring to attain a male body;
this is the fifth.
Furthermore, sisters:
If a woman accomplishes six qualities, she will transform her female body and obtain a male body.
What are these six?
They are: being swift and supple.
Upright and straightforward;
without hypocrisy;
without illusion.
To be without deceit and to possess a mind of uprightness—
this is the sixth.
"Furthermore, sisters!
If women accomplish seven dharmas, they shall transform their female bodies and attain the state of men.
What are these seven?
That is to say: one constantly recollects the Buddha because one desires to attain the Buddha-body;
one constantly recollects the True Dharma because one desires to attain the Buddha-Dharma;
and one constantly and perpetually recollects the Sangha because one desires to personally realize the Sangha.
One constantly and eternally recollects the precepts because of the purity of one's vows;
one constantly and eternally recollects relinquishment because of the abandonment of all afflictions;
and one constantly and eternally recollects the heavens because of the clear realization of the bodhicitta.
"Because they observe all sentient beings with a heart of joy—
this is the seventh.
Furthermore, sisters!"
If a woman accomplishes eight dharmas, she transforms her female body into a male body.
What are these eight?
She does not crave food, nor does she crave feasting and drinking.
He does not crave men;
he does not crave powdered incense or unguents;
he does not crave wandering through and viewing gardens and groves.
He does not crave jesting and laughter;
he does not crave the sounds of song or various musical performances;
he does not crave dancing and play.
Not craving the pleasure of social gatherings with wine—
this is the eighth.
"Furthermore, sisters!
If a woman accomplishes nine dharmas, she will transform her female body and obtain a male body.
What are these nine?
She does not speak of a self.
It does not say that there are sentient beings;
it does not say that there is a life-force, nor a person, nor a man.
It does not speak of the view of annihilationism.
He does not speak of the view of eternalism;
he does not cling to the view of existence,
nor does he cling to the view of non-existence.
"Skillfully understanding the law of causes and conditions— this is the ninth.
Furthermore, sisters!"
If a woman accomplishes ten dharmas, she will transform her female body and obtain a male body, swiftly attaining Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
What are these ten?
One practices a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings;
one does not give rise to covetous desire for the wealth and possessions of others;
and one does not think of other men.
Even at the cost of one's life, one shall never speak falsely;
one shall not engage in divisive speech,
nor in harsh or abusive speech.
One does not engage in meaningless speech;
one does not give rise to ignorance;
and one is not dragged away by anger.
"Sisters! To have upright views based on the retribution of karma—
this is the tenth dharma by which a woman, having accomplished these ten dharmas, transforms her female body and attains a male body, quickly realizing Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Furthermore, sisters!
A woman should contemplate the profound Dharma.
She should contemplate form as being like foam on water, and thus not become intoxicated by or greedy for form;

One contemplates feelings as being like bubbles: within pleasant feelings, one does not give rise to craving or attachment; within painful feelings, one does not abandon them through aversion; and within neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings, one does not give rise to the fetter of delusion.
One contemplates perceptions as being like a mirage, wherein one does not give rise to notions of "male" or "female.

One contemplates mental formations as being like a plantain tree, understanding that all formations lack any solid core; having contemplated thus, one does not dwell upon any phenomena and does not give rise to conceptual attachments.
One contemplates consciousness as being like an illusion, understanding that the mental consciousness is like a phantom person who has come.
Having known this, one is entirely unstained by any phenomena.

One contemplates and knows that this body is a combination of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—and that what is formed by these elements is conventionally designated as a "body," being just like grass, trees, walls, or rubble.

This body is like a shadow; it is without self, without sentient beings, without life-force, without a person, and without a male principle. It revolves by itself through the workings of karma; the delusions regarding the various elements are like an empty village.
One contemplates the eye as it truly is: merely a lump of flesh, its nature empty and quiescent;

likewise, one correctly contemplates the nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as empty and quiescent. One understands the body to be like a reflection in a mirror, understands speech to be like an echo, and contemplates the mind as an illusion.
"Thus it is, sisters!
If women contemplate all dharmas in this manner, they will swiftly transform their female bodies into male bodies and quickly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

At that time, the queen and the court ladies of the Great Tree Kinnara King, having heard the Buddha preach this Dharma for transforming the female body, were filled with unprecedented joy and exultation upon hearing this Dharma gate; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and remained there with sincere devotion, refusing to rise.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the various queens of the Kinnara King, smiled.

It is the constant law of the Buddha that when he smiles, hundreds of thousands of rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and purple—issue forth from his mouth, illuminating immeasurable and boundless worlds. Reaching upward as far as the Brahma world, they eclipse the light of the sun and moon; then returning, they abide before the Buddha, circumambulate him three times, and enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, spoke these verses:
"I ask the stainless one whose face is joyful; I ask the stainless one of exceptional majesty and virtue;
I ask the one well-able to sever all doubts: For what reason do you smile?"
I ask the one who maintains purity and possesses the most wondrous form; I ask the one who is able to benefit the world;
I ask the one who is supreme among humans and devas: out of compassion for whom do you manifest this smile?
I ask the one who delights in giving and is well-tamed; I ask the one who delights in upholding the pure precepts;
I ask the one who delights in patience and has attained the power of forbearance: for what benefit do you manifest this smile?
I ask him who abides in the power of diligence; I ask him who dwells in dhyāna and possesses supernormal powers;
I ask him whose wisdom is equal to space: for what reason, O Peerless One, do you manifest a smile?
I ask the Sugata of great compassionate heart; I ask the one of great pity who pities the world;
I ask the one who delights in joy and great equanimity: by what causes and conditions do you manifest this smile?
I ask: you who have crossed to the further shore of the three impurities; I ask: you who are stainless and possess the pure three eyes;
I ask: you who dwell in the constant bliss of the three gates of liberation—for what reason do you manifest this smile?
I ask the one who can subdue all opposing hosts; I ask the one who can preach the nectar-like Dharma;
I ask the one who can darken all Māras— O Great Compassionate One, pray tell me the cause and condition for your smile!
I ask the one who upholds the supreme ten powers; I ask the one whose complexion is like a mountain of gold;
I ask the one who has reached the pinnacle of merit: for what benefit have you manifested this smile?
At that time, the Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Do you now see these consorts of the Great Tree Kinnara King?

Having planted roots of goodness before me, they have sincerely resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, desiring to transform their female bodies to take on male bodies as they prostrate at my feet.”
Ānanda replied,
“I have seen it, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"The consorts of the Kinnara King, through this sincere devotion, have planted various roots of goodness; at the end of their lives here, they will cast off their female bodies, attain male forms, and be born in Tuṣita Heaven, where they shall together with Maitreya Bodhisattva protect the unsurpassed, true, and correct Dharma accumulated by me over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas."

One shall further make offerings to Maitreya when he attains Buddhahood, and in this successive manner, one shall make offerings to all the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, gradually fulfilling the factors that assist the path to enlightenment.
When this Great Tree Kinnara King attains Buddhahood, these women shall be born in his land, and that Buddha-Tathāgata shall bestow upon them their prophecy of enlightenment.
At that time, the Great Kinnara King Druma addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has performed a great work of Buddhahood for us: he has cleared away the evil realms and established us in the good realms; he has shown us the path to Bodhi and dwells within the great jewel-treasury of wisdom; he has brought to fulfillment all supramundane roots of goodness and spoken of the companions that assist in the accomplishment of the *pāramitās*; he has shown skillful means and exhorted us toward the Bodhicitta, so that we are fully satisfied by hearing the Dharma; we have obtained instruction, benefit, joy, and delight in the profound Dharma, and have all attained stable dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression.”
World-Honored One!
We shall now act as those who recognize your kindness and not as those who fail to recognize it.
World-Honored One!
"At this time, if we were to offer even our flesh, blood, marrow, and brain, we would still not repay his kindness; how much less so with other precious treasures?
At that time, there was another bodhisattva in the assembly who thought to himself:
"When will this Great Tree Kinnara King attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Upon attaining Buddhahood, what will be his name?
How will that Buddha-land be adorned?
And by what means will the assembly of bodhisattvas be adorned?
"And what are the characteristics of the objects he enjoys?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of this bodhisattva, smiled.

From his face, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rays of light of various colors issued forth, universally illuminating Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions. Having brought rest to the suffering of all sentient beings, they traveled everywhere through the world of devas and returned to circle the Buddha. After completing one thousand circumambulations, they entered through the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and stood before the Tathāgata with palms joined, speaking these verses:
“I prostrate to the Sugata, who has never before displayed A smile with such signs and characteristics;
It illuminates immeasurable billions of worlds, Throughout the ten directions like the sands of the Ganges.”
The radiance of Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors, as well as the light of the sun, moon, pearls, and fire— All these are completely eclipsed by the light of the Honored One among Men;
I pray that you will explain for what cause and condition you smile.
The three evil realms are stilled and their various sufferings extinguished; sentient beings, freed from fetters, attain joy.
Humans, devas, and all other beings obtain happiness—O Pure One, for what reason do you smile?
Who among those dwelling in the Great Vehicle—whether humans or devas—is destined to realize the turning of the Wheel of Dharma?
Who has attained the fulfillment of supreme Bodhi? Who, being courageous and steadfast, emits this pure and wondrous light?
Dharma King, we pray that you sever our doubts, so that all other devas may likewise be free from uncertainty;
the great assembly rejoices and desires to hear: for whose sake have you manifested this smile?
At that time, after Ānanda had questioned the Buddha with these verses, he circumambulated him three times to the right and returned to his original seat.
Then the World-Honored One, like a great dragon, looked out over the ten directions and addressed Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda!
"Do you now see this Great Tree Kinnara King making such vast and extensive offerings to the Tathāgata?
Ānanda replied, "I have seen them."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“After sixty-eight hundred thousand billion kalpas have passed, this Great Tree Kinnara King shall attain Buddhahood, to be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, World-Honored One, named Guṇarājaprabhāsa.”
The name of the land is Stainless Moon, and the eon is named Possessing Jewels. Ānanda!

The ground of this world-system Stainless Moon is as level as the palm of a hand; it is made of white lapis lazuli, as pure and stainless as the color of the moon. It is free from thorns, potsherds, gravel, and stones, and there are exquisite jeweled terraces abiding in mid-air, where the bodhisattvas walk back and forth upon the ground.
At that time, images of the World-Honored Tathāgatas, King of Merit Radiance, appeared on both sides; upon seeing these images of the Tathāgatas, those bodhisattvas immediately attained this thought:
"All dharmas are likewise like these images."

"If there are sentient beings who have doubts regarding the Dharma, they shall immediately question the Buddha-image; having questioned the Buddha-image, they will be able to receive and uphold it, attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
All sentient beings shall dwell supported by this precious pavilion of empty space."
In that Buddha-land, there is not even the name "woman," and all the sentient beings therein are born through transformation.
In that land, there is not even the name for food and drink; they subsist solely on the food of the joy of Dharma.
In that land, there are no other vehicles; it is purely the One Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), and all sentient beings are definitively established in the Mahāyāna.
Among those beings, there are none who violate the prohibitions or fail in proper deportment, nor any who destroy right view; all sentient beings are definitively established in the Buddha-dharma.

In that land, there are no Māras, nor Māra-devas, nor heterodox teachers such as the Nirgranthas; they do not cling to various views, nor even abide in or cling to "right views. All sentient beings therein are sealed by the profound practice of the seal of emptiness.
Among those sentient beings, there was no distinction between humans and devas, and all that they enjoyed was entirely equal.

The lifespan of that Tathāgata King of Merit and Radiance was ten intermediate kalpas; he brought great benefit and great peace and happiness, benefiting and bringing peace to devas and humans, and his retinue of immeasurable bodhisattvas was for the most part non-retrogressive.
"When that Tathāgata Guṇarājaprabhāsa was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he bestowed a prediction upon the Bodhisattva Uttaratīkṣṇavīrya, saying:
'O Bodhisattva Uttaratīkṣṇavīrya!'"
"After me, you shall attain Buddhahood and be known as the Tathāgata Mahāvyūha, and so forth, up to Buddha, World-Honored One.
Within this kalpa, the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha will never be interrupted; therefore, this kalpa is named "Possessing Jewels" (Ratnasaṃbhava).

At that time, the Great Kinnara King Druma, having heard his own prediction of enlightenment, was filled with unprecedented joy and leaped for gladness. By the power of the roots of goodness of a great bodhisattva and desiring to inspire a heart of joy and increase the roots of goodness in the great assembly, he ascended into the air to the height of seven *tāla* trees. Through the Buddha’s spiritual power and by means of his own eloquence, he spoke these verses:
“The true nature universally encompasses all phenomena; Its nature is like space, free from defilement.
Having realized this wondrous Way, One becomes the eldest son of all Buddhas.”
Just as that which is seen in a dream has no reality and is entirely illusory, so too,
having understood all phenomena to be like dreams, one feels neither sorrow nor aversion toward conditioned formations.
