Just as the manifestations produced by illusion— The hosts of troops consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—
Have no reality within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), So too these aggregates (*skandha*) are like illusions, lacking any solidity or substance.
The essential nature of form is like foam on water; All sensations appear like bubbles;
Perception is like a mirage in the heat; Volitional formations lack reality, like the trunk of a plantain tree.
The three—the mind with its mental factors and consciousness— The Tathāgata says are like illusions and transformations;
Knowing that the nature of the aggregates is empty and non-existent, One feels no weariness amidst all conditioned formations.
The four great elements and all realms are like the Dharma-realm; the sense bases are comparable to an empty village.
Having understood all phenomena in this way, one is able to uphold the treasury of the Buddhas’ emptiness-dharma.
Skillfully self-subduing through the giving of wealth, One self-subdues by means of pure precepts that are empty;
The nature of patience is eternally exhausted and signless, Vigor is supreme and wondrously ever-extinguished.
The nature of dhyāna is quiescent and free from conceptual proliferation; wisdom, too, is empty, quiescent, and free from conceptual proliferation.
If one can enter into such a Dharma, this is called "crossing over to the other shore."
Loving-kindness is without self and without sentient beings; Great compassion is pure like space;
Great joy and great equanimity are entirely empty and still— This path, the Brahma-path, is eternally supreme.
These four integrations are the most supreme; the Tathāgata has taught that they can universally integrate all.
Through these integrations and that which is integrated, one attains eternal liberation; such a person reaches the further shore of the dharma of integration.
Sentient beings have no self and no sentient beings; One cannot find a life-span or a person.
The six sense faculties are always characterized by natural quiescence; One who can know this is called a Bodhisattva!
There are no bodhisattvas and no sentient beings, nor does one give rise to the conceit of "non-existence";
being free from these two extremes, unattached and without conceptual proliferation—such a one is called a truly unattached bodhisattva!
All phenomena lack reality, like floating clouds; there is neither one who comes nor one who goes.
Their essence eternally abides in the nature of the Dharma-realm; the Sugata has awakened to this suchness.
All phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent; All phenomena exist by virtue of causes and conditions.
Like lightning that flashes briefly and then vanishes, One’s mind should always delight in contemplating them thus.
The activities of the mind are non-material and cannot be grasped; the world is likewise equally ungraspable.
If one knows that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure, there will be no fetters or any darkness.
One speaks of the body as being like wood or like a wall; it is deluded and without a master, like rubble.
Having thus understood its fundamental nature, one no longer forms a mind that relies upon the body.
The speech of the mouth is pure like the wind, like an echo in a mountain valley;
knowing all sounds to be thus, one is not stained by desire for those sounds.
Dwelling in emptiness, one does not fall; Emptiness has no abode and no location.
Having known that all phenomena are like space, Sentient beings likewise abide in suchness.
Space is fundamentally without birth or burning; even for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, it is not burned.
Knowing that all phenomena are like space, one reaches hundreds of thousands of realms free from burning.
Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa mountains, and all other peaks;
great cities, villages, towns, and grasses and trees—able to know these as being like empty space, their supernormal powers reach as far as a thousand billion worlds.
The earth element, water, fire, and the wind element—these four great elements are like space;
one who can know that all these are equal will, with courageous vigor, traverse billions of realms through the void.
All sounds existing within the three realms— whether supreme and sublime, or middling and inferior—
even if spoken for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, one does not perceive their intrinsic nature nor know where they abide.
That supreme state has no distinct characteristics; though known, it cannot be awakened to by the mind.
When the mind and mental factors equally enter into tranquility, all Tathāgatas are equal in their Dharma.
Having cultivated roots of goodness for hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, Originally practicing as a bodhisattva;
Knowing that awakening is identical to all phenomena, That one of great renown receives the prediction of enlightenment.
The nature of the realm of all phenomena is inherently pure; the realm of the Tathāgata is immeasurable.
Having thus realized this equality, one who upholds such virtues receives the prophecy of enlightenment.
Now I have no aggregate of form or feeling; the aggregates of perception, volition, and formations are likewise so!
Having understood and realized awakening, I receive the prediction; I do not receive a prediction regarding the aggregates, nor a prediction regarding the elements or sense bases.
The patience they have attained is fundamentally empty and quiescent; patience and exhaustion are equal and non-dual.
This is the immeasurable patience of non-arising; thus, one receives the prophecy.
There is nothing that can exhaust the inexhaustible; by exhausting all inquiry, one does not give rise to any phenomena.
Having attained the penetration of patience, one receives the prediction of enlightenment; there are no phrases, yet one enters into phrases, for there is no sign.
In reality, there is no number and no two extremes; there is no distinct agent, nor is there anything that is to be made real.
If it is thus, the Buddha grants the prediction: "Now my nature is equal to all phenomena."
One's own nature is selfless and empty, and the nature of bodhi is like space;
if one can receive a prediction of enlightenment in such a manner, this is called wrong practice, not right practice.
If one practices with mind and intention, performing superior deeds within the dharma of equality;
such as these all dwell upon the ground, while I now dwell above in the midst of space.
"Knowing that those dwelling on the stages are not equal, And that their wisdom increases as they do not cling to the three realms;
For this reason, they receive the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Great Tree Kinnara King descended from the void, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him thus:
“World-Honored One!
You have performed the Buddha-work for my sake and bestowed upon me the prediction of the fulfillment of the unsurpassed path.
World-Honored One!”
"The various practices I cultivated in past lives have not been in vain; I have not deceived myself regarding the practices I performed.
At that time, within the great assembly, there was a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who thought to himself:
"This is the Great Tree Kinnara King!"
"Under which Buddha did they first plant the roots of goodness?
What was the name of that Tathāgata?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tiara-King (Devamukuṭa), knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, addressed them, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Under which Buddha did this Great Tree Kinnara King first plant roots of goodness and resolve his mind toward Bodhi?
What was the name of that World-Honored Buddha?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Tiara-Crown: "Good son!

In the past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and again beyond immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there was a Buddha named Ratnaskandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and so forth, up to Buddha, World-Honored One."
This Buddha-world is named Pure Adornment, and its eon is named Pure and Clean.

This Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaskandha has a community of sixty billion bodhisattvas, all of whom possess immeasurable diligence, have attained dhāraṇīs, and do not regress from the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
The lifespan of that Buddha is sixty billion years.

All the objects of enjoyment within that land are fully provided and composed entirely of lapis lazuli; like the Tuṣita Heaven, food and drink are abundant, and there is no other vehicle in the land—only the Single Great Vehicle.

"At that time, there was a great Wheel-Turning King named Nimiṃdhara, who held sovereign power over the four quarters. He possessed forty thousand consorts and a full complement of a thousand sons, who were valiant, of exquisite appearance, and capable of subduing all opposing hosts."

At that time, King Nimiṃdhara invited the Tathāgata Ratnaskandha and the assembly of bodhisattvas, and for a full one hundred million years, he provided all necessities—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and every kind of pleasant requisite—performing such immeasurable offerings.

Having made offerings to the Tathāgata, they have already cultivated these roots of goodness; furthermore, forty thousand ladies, along with their thousands of sons, and eighty-four thousand other sentient beings, have all together resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Having resolved his mind upon the path, he further spent a full hundred million years constantly making offerings of all manner of delightful requisites to the Tathāgata Ratnaskandha.

After this period had passed, he abdicated the royal throne in favor of his eldest son, named Śīlavant, and having relinquished the sovereignty of the kingdom, he shaved off his hair and beard and went forth into homelessness out of faith within that Buddha’s Dharma.

In this way, the thousand sons successively abdicated their thrones to one another and each went forth into the homeless life, with the sole exception of the youngest prince named Juebei (Awakened Compassion), who ruled the country according to the True Dharma without the use of weapons, governing the realm with perfect mastery and sovereignty.

“Good son! At that time, once King Nimiṃdhara and his sons had gone forth, they were able to receive and uphold all the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃcaya at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.”
Good son! What do you think?
Is this not another person?
Do not harbor any doubts.
That Cakravartin King Nimiṃdhara is none other than the present Great Tree Kinnara King.
As for that king’s sons, they are all these good men who are now practicing the bodhisattva path.

The Great Tree Kinnara King first conceived the aspiration for unexcelled bodhicitta within the Dharma of that Ratnaskandha Tathāgata; from that time forth, he never ceased seeing Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and making offerings to the Saṅgha, while teaching and transforming sentient beings, yet he did not swiftly take up the path of unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
"I now bestow upon you this prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment; you shall become a Buddha named Guṇarājaprabhāsa Tathāgata.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tiara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"It is unprecedented! The wisdom of the Tathāgata is inconceivable, for he is able to know such a vast duration of time.
The Buddha said, "It is so."
Good son! As you have said, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are immeasurable and boundless. Why is this?
"Good son!

Regarding all sentient beings of the past, immeasurable in number, the Tathāgata is able to know all their minds—where they were, in what manner, and what they did, whether their karma was wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; the Tathāgata knows all such movements of mind.

Furthermore, regarding the minds that arise in the present—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—the Tathāgata knows them all, including where they are in the ten directions, in what manner, and what they do."
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses such unimpeded knowledge and vision;
whatever thoughts all sentient beings in future ages may give rise to, the Tathāgata knows them all.

When this discourse on the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom was being spoken, thirty-two thousand sentient beings who had not previously resolved their minds now for the first time earnestly gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, after the Great Tree Kinnara King had completed seven nights of providing offerings to the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and the great assembly of śrāvakas, he further offered all necessary musical instruments, as well as his palaces, gardens, groves, and grounds, saying:

"I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will deign to come here frequently out of compassion for me; it shall bring great peace and happiness, and great benefit to all the gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas."
At that time, the prince of the Great Tree Kinnaras named Vimalanetra offered a net of precious jewels to the Tathāgata and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
We kinnaras are intoxicated by the fragrance of flowers, intoxicated by song and dance, and intoxicated by joy.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will expound for us the Dharma-gate of entry!
"May we cause ourselves to abandon this mad intoxication and cultivate and gather the dharmas that assist the path to enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Kinnara prince Vimalanetra: "Worthy one!"
From this time forth, I shall protect you and cause all musical instruments to produce the sounds of the sixty-four sublime dharmas that assist awakening.
What are these sixty-four?

That is to say, the sound of the performance of generosity, the sound of ethical discipline, the sound of patience, the sound of diligence, the sound of meditative concentration, and the sound of wisdom;
the sound of loving-kindness, the sound of compassion, the sound of sympathetic joy, and the sound of equanimity.
The sound of the four means of attraction; the sound of never forgetting the unsurpassed bodhicitta; the sound of not wearying of birth and death; the sound of gathering roots of goodness;
the sound of the Buddha; the sound of the Dharma; and the sound of the Sangha of bhikṣus.

The sound of the foundations of mindfulness, the sound of the right efforts, the sound of the bases of psychic power, the sound of the faculties, the sound of the powers, the sound of the factors of awakening, and the sound of the path;
the sound of concentration and the sound of wisdom.
The sound of impermanence, the sound of suffering, the sound of non-self;
the sound of tranquility, the sound of non-activity, the sound of stillness, the sound of non-arising, the sound of non-origination;
the sound of suchness, the sound of the dharma-nature, and the sound of the limit of reality.
The sound of non-self; the sound of no sentient beings; the sound of no life-principle.
The sound of no person; the sound of no individual; the sound of no coming; the sound of no going; the sound of no place; the sound of no abiding.
The sound of emptiness, the sound of signlessness, the sound of wishlessness;
the sound of detachment, the sound of cessation, the sound of non-existence, and the sound of dependent origination;

the sound of the absence of things, the sound of the absence of accumulation, the sound of the absence of dependence, the sound of protecting the True Dharma, the sound of subduing Māra, the sound of skillful means, the sound of teaching and transforming sentient beings, the sound that is like an illusion, a transformation, lightning, the moon in water, a dream, or an echo; the sound of the destruction of the dharma-realm, the sound of acting according to what is spoken, and the sound of gathering all roots of goodness without forgetting them or being heedless.
Thus it is, worthy sirs!

I shall cause such sounds as these sixty-four kinds of dharmas that protect and assist the path to enlightenment to issue forth from all your musical instruments; I shall cause you to attain non-negligence and fulfill the dharmas that assist enlightenment.
The Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā Sūtra, Volume Three.
The Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā Sūtra, Volume Four.
Translated by Kumārajīva, Tripiṭaka Master of Kucha during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
At that time, the entire great assembly attained what they had never experienced before; with palms joined in reverence, they prostrated to the Buddha and spoke these words:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
“The Tathāgata is indeed able to skillfully protect and mindfully sustain all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, sustaining them through his power of supernormal knowledges.
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is!”
As you have said, the Tathāgata protects and keeps all bodhisattvas in mind.
Why is this? To protect and keep bodhisattvas in mind is precisely to protect and keep all sentient beings in mind.
O you noble sons!
If the Buddha-Tathāgata protects bodhisattvas, he thereby protects all sentient beings. Why is this?

This bodhisattva, for the sake of all sentient beings, undertakes the great armor; having donned this great armor, he causes immeasurable sentient beings to leave behind the hunger of birth and death, uproots them from it, and establishes them securely in the right path.
"O noble sons!
For this reason, after my parinirvāṇa, you should protect all bodhisattvas; know that if you protect a bodhisattva, you have already protected all sentient beings."
If a bodhisattva gives clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine for the sick, this is equivalent to giving them to all sentient beings.
If one gives articles of pleasure to a bodhisattva, it is as if one has already given them to all sentient beings.
"Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas constantly exhalate and inhalate for the sake of all sentient beings.

At that time, the devas of the desire realm, the devas of the form realm, the gandharvas, the mahoragas, and the great assembly, hearing what the Buddha had said, rejoiced from the depths of their hearts. They scattered various exquisite flowers, precious gems, necklaces, and diverse powdered incenses over the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Great Tree Kinnara King thought to himself:

"Now that the Tathāgata, along with the bodhisattvas and the great assembly of śrāvakas, are about to return, I shall use my supernatural power to go forth from here and create a great precious chariot for the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and the great assembly of śrāvakas to mount and travel upon. I and my retinue shall together pull the chariot; thus will I fulfill my offerings to the Tathāgata."

At that time, having formed this thought, the Great Kinnara King Druma immediately fashioned a precious chariot out of celestial jewels. It was five yojanas in height, and its length and breadth were likewise exactly five yojanas. It was inlaid with various jewels and adorned with immeasurable jewel trees. Upon this chariot, he constructed a lion throne for the Buddha Tathāgata; it was exquisitely decorated and stood seven *ṛṇu* high, spread with immeasurable celestial jewel robes. He also prepared seats for all the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, and for the sake of those listening to the Dharma, he provided seats for all the devaputras, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), gandharvas, and others.
At that time, having prepared a great precious chariot and arranged various seats, the Kinnara King joined his palms and said:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One and the great assembly will take their seats upon the precious chariot out of compassion for me."
At that time, the World-Honored One, along with the assembly of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and all other beings, sat upon seats spread within the precious chariot.

Then, by the spiritual power of the Buddha and his own spiritual power, the Kinnara King placed this precious chariot in the palm of his right hand and ascended into the air to a height of seven tala trees.
The eight thousand sons of the Kinnara King, along with immeasurable gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, each pulling the precious chariot with golden chains, traveled through the air.
Eighty-four thousand kinnaras performed eighty-four thousand kinds of music as they proceeded before the Tathāgata to lead the way, praising the Buddha with these verses:
“Fully eighty thousand and four thousand Are the bodies of these kinnaras;
With pure and wondrous songs harmonizing with various instruments, They praise the true merits of the Tathāgata.”
Possessing the most excellent marks and signs with majestic power, With the most excellent and wondrous form beloved by all;
Ever abiding in pure and true merit— The World-Honored One possesses such great merit.
Standing in the sky above, attending at his left and right, none are able to see the Tathāgata’s crown;
like a great mountain, firm and immovable, such is the body endowed with qualities that bring joy.
Wandering through space with sovereign ease wherever he goes, the Guide possesses such great supernormal power;
like the void, pure and stainless, the World-Honored One has skillfully severed and liberated himself from the fetters and latent tendencies.
The asuras and rākṣasas, Śakra, Brahmā, the celestial kings, and those of the Pure Abodes;
the sun, moon, stars, pearls, and fire—all were completely eclipsed by the radiance of the ūrṇā-kośa.
The power of your wisdom is like the great ocean, Arousing the various mental activities of sentient beings;
With the three types of knowledge, you universally illumine the three realms— I pay homage with my head bowed to you, who are honored by the world.
Having subdued the four māras and all fetters, he proclaims the Four Noble Truths and the path to nirvāṇa;
with the four bases of power, the powers, and the fearlessnesses, the Tathāgata’s stride is most preeminent.
Advancing slowly and steadily without wavering, they constantly practice mental cultivation and abide in samādhi;
their subtle and wondrous teachings delight the world, yet they do not rely upon those very words.
Your speech is gentle, with a voice that is excellent and sublime; it is heard afar throughout immeasurable lands.
If there are sentient beings who hear this sound, they all find peace and give rise to joy.
The waters of all oceans within the three thousandfold world system are entirely contained within a single pore;
yet they never disturb or harm the sentient beings living in the water, for his power of spiritual penetrations remains undiminished.
All the mountains within the three thousandfold world system, he places entirely within a single hair;
though he travels to immeasurable billions of worlds, his physical strength suffers no diminution.
Furthermore, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, you diligently practiced boundless austerities and the giving of self-mastery;
you skillfully cultivated and trained in the precepts to guard the sense faculties, and perfected the powers of patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom.
Making offerings to immeasurable billions of Buddhas, They uphold and protect what these Buddhas have taught;
Their minds never give rise to weariness or fatigue, As they benefit the world with great kindness and great compassion.
Not humbled within the unconditioned, nor exalting oneself within the conditioned;
like the great earth, unmoving and unshakable, one dwells amidst worldly dharmas like a lotus flower.
Contemplating thoroughly, one realizes all phenomena are empty; They are entirely without marks, like the moon in water;
Like illusions, like transformations, like bubbles on water, And like the appearances of dreams, lightning, and mirages.
In true nature there is no self and no person; it is utterly pure, unburnt, and without a master.
Like space, it is pure and stainless; all existing things are of this true nature.
All causes and conditions, and the phenomena that flow and form, have no master;
one who can fully awaken to this path of bodhi is therefore called a Buddha.
These sentient beings obtain great benefit, whether they see the Teacher or hear [his teaching];
they shall never fear falling into the evil realms, for such people always reach the good paths.
We have now obtained the opportunity to make offerings to the Superior One! All shall offer, and I too shall offer;
dedicating this toward the bodhicitta, may all beings become like the Honored One among Men!
Even if one could measure the void, And exhaust the waters of the great ocean with a single hair-tip;
Even if the sun, moon, and stars were to fall from the sky, No one could ever exhaust the virtues of the Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One traveled through the air riding upon a precious chariot, emitting golden light. This light shone everywhere throughout this trichiliocosm; within the great city of Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain, the illumination was twice as bright.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Rājagṛha, together with his queen, retinue, and military forces, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, brahmins, and householders, having witnessed this auspicious omen of light, took various incense, flowers, powdered incense, unguents, banners, flags, precious parasols, and musical instruments, and departed from Rājagṛha to go out and welcome the Tathāgata.

Having already departed from the city, he went to Vulture Peak Mountain; there he heard from afar the subtle and exquisite sounds of music and song produced by the kinnaras, which filled the entirety of Vulture Peak Mountain.
At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the Great Tree Kinnara King descended from the void with a great precious chariot and set it down within Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
At that time, the World-Honored One descended from his precious chariot and proceeded to his own residence, where he spread out his seat and sat down.
Then the bodhisattvas and the great assembly of śrāvakas also all descended from their vehicles, prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata, and sat down in order.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, along with his queen, court ladies, and inner and outer retinues, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, brahmins, and householders, each offered the various articles of worship they had brought to the Tathāgata. Kneeling on their right knees with palms joined, they paid their respects, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Are you not weary?
Have you traveled in safety?
Having finished these greetings, he withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Diadem-Adorned addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How much merit shall the Great Tree Kinnara King and his host of Kinnaras obtain for having drawn the Tathāgata’s chariot through the air to this place?"
The Buddha said,

“Good son! This Great Tree Kinnara King and his other followers who have resolved their minds on the Path shall, from this day forward, attain the five supernormal powers and continue until they achieve Buddhahood.”

From one buddha-field to another, they never cease seeing the Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and making offerings to the Sangha. In every lifetime in which they are born, they constantly remember their past lives; they attain excellent eloquence and beautiful voices, and they never abandon the transformation of sentient beings. In every lifetime in which they are born, they diligently protect the True Dharma and diligently transform sentient beings.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru said to the Kinnara King Mahādruma: "Kinnara King!
You have truly attained excellent benefit, for the Tathāgata now praises your meritorious virtues."
“Kinnara King!
I too hope to share even a small portion of your merit.
Then, the Great Tree Kinnara King spoke to King Ajātaśatru:
"Great King, you should know that all the merits I possess, I bestow entirely upon you and all sentient beings.
Why is this? Great King!"
Whatever meritorious deeds a bodhisattva possesses, he shares them entirely with all sentient beings.
Why is this? Great King!
The Dharma of a bodhisattva is free from all stinginess; they bestow all their merits upon sentient beings, their minds joyful, without feverish passion or affliction.
Great King, you should know that the bodhisattva dedicates these merits toward omniscience and for the sake of nurturing all sentient beings.
Why is this? Great King!
Because Bodhisattvas protect and mind all sentient beings, they practice for enlightenment to serve as a refuge for those beings.
"Great King!

You too have now attained great and excellent benefit: having obtained the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and Mañjuśrī as your spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), you have approached them and heard the Dharma. Thus, unreal ignorance, the obscuring veil of darkness, the sins of immediate retribution, doubt, and the fever of affliction have been extinguished, and you have attained the great light of the Dharma.
Because you have attained this light of the Dharma, you abide in peace and security, free from all distress and heat."
Therefore, Great King!

You should exert yourself and discipline yourself to become a vessel for the Dharma; if you hear even a single phrase of the Dharma and do not forget or lose it, this is called "protecting the True Dharma."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Tiānguān addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many dharmas must a bodhisattva accomplish to be able to serve as a vessel for the Dharma?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Tiānguān:
“Good son! There are thirty-two vessels for the Bodhisattva Dharma.”
What are these thirty-two?
Being sustained by the Buddha is the vessel for bodhicitta.
Single-minded sincerity and straightforwardness are the vessel for being without hypocrisy.
Increasing one's resolve is the vessel for the roots of goodness.
Practicing the Path is the vessel for the pillar of bodhi.
Right mental attention is the vessel for extensive learning.
Wisdom is the vessel for the path of transcendence;
diligence is the vessel for accumulating righteousness;
generosity is the vessel for great wealth.
Ethical discipline is the vessel for fulfilling vows;
patience is the vessel for the thirty-two marks of a great man;
and diligence is the vessel for all Buddha-dharmas.
Dhyāna is the vessel for refining the mind;
Prajñā is the vessel for transcending obstacles;
Great Compassion is the vessel for equalizing all sentient beings.
Great compassion is the vessel for rescuing and uprooting poverty;
great joy is the vessel for delighting in the Buddha-dharma;
great equanimity is the vessel for relinquishing both attachment and aversion.
A virtuous friend is the vessel for all roots of goodness;
cultivating progress and extensive learning is the vessel for the Prajñāpāramitā;
and leaving the household life is the vessel for liberation from bondage and obstruction.
The forest hermitage is the vessel for having few affairs and being free from disturbance;
delighting in tranquility is the vessel for all meditative concentrations and supernormal powers;
the four means of integration are the vessel for transforming sentient beings.
Upholding all dharmas is the vessel of illumination;
dharanis are the vessel for hearing all that has not yet been heard;
and eloquence is the vessel for severing all doubts.
Mindfulness of the Buddha is the vessel for beholding all Buddhas;
a mind free from affliction and harm is the vessel for protecting all roots of goodness;
and the dharma of emptiness is the vessel for severing the view of self.
The causal conditions are the vessel for relinquishing all that is cherished;
the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is the vessel for relinquishing all obstacles and receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*);
and the stage of non-retrogression is the vessel of fearlessness.
“Good son! These are the thirty-two vessels of the Bodhisattva.
When this Dharma was being taught, ten thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that all sentient beings may become such vessels of the Dharma, and that we ourselves may also become such vessels of the Dharma, just as the Buddha has taught.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great Tree Kinnara King:
“Good son! Return to your dwelling; might your kinsmen not be filled with anxiety?
The Kinnara king replied:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva were to experience sorrow and dejection, they would not be called a ‘bodhisattva. Why is this?
"Bhagavān! One who is able to endure sorrow and dejection is called a bodhisattva.
Bhagavān!"
"How is it that a bodhisattva experiences sorrow and dejection?
How is it that a bodhisattva is free from sorrow and dejection?
The Buddha told the Kinnara King:
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will experience anxiety and distress, which they should recognize.
What are these four?
Upon hearing that there are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, their mind gives rise to alarm and fear."
Upon hearing of immeasurable and boundless birth and death, his mind gives rise to alarm and fear;
upon hearing of the immeasurable wisdom of the Buddha-Tathāgata, his mind gives rise to alarm and fear;
upon hearing of the accumulation of immeasurable merit and adornment that fulfills the marks and signs of excellence, his mind gives rise to alarm and fear.
"Kinnara King!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they experience sorrow and distress. Kinnara King!"
A bodhisattva who accomplishes four dharmas will have a mind free from sorrow and dejection; this should be understood.
What are the four?
Hearing that there are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, one thinks, "I shall establish them all on the path to nirvana," and remains without sorrow or dejection.
Hearing of the immeasurable cycle of birth and death, one is not startled or afraid; cultivating all roots of goodness, the mind is free from sorrow or dejection.
Having heard of the immeasurable wisdom of the Buddha-Tathāgata, one thinks: "I shall fulfill such great wisdom as this," and remains free from sorrow or dejection.
Hearing that one will attain the marks and signs of physical perfection through the accumulation of immeasurable merit and adornments,
yet remaining free from anxiety or dejection— this is the fourth. "Kinnara King!
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who has accomplished four dharmas should recognize that they possess anxiety.
What are these four?
At times they desire to realize the Śrāvaka vehicle, and at times they desire to realize the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
"When the Dharma is about to perish, one abandons it rather than protecting and upholding it, and does not exhort others to abide in Bodhi.
These are the four.
O King of Kinnaras!"
Furthermore, a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas through which they are free from anxiety; these should be understood.
What are the four?
When faced with urgent suffering, they do not abandon the bodhicitta.
They do not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
They would rather sacrifice their own body and life than abandon the True Dharma.
Even beyond a distance of one hundred yojanas, they exhort others to resolve upon bodhicitta.
These are the four. "Kinnara King!
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva accomplishes four other dharmas, they will experience anxiety and dejection; these should be recognized."
What are the four?
Seeing a beggar come, one gives rise to anger and scolds them;
one delights in lying down in comfort for oneself.
Not cultivating extensive learning;
and having heard the Dharma, not explaining it for the sake of the assembly—
these are the four.
“Kinnara King! Furthermore, there are four dharmas that a bodhisattva accomplishes such that he is free from anxiety and dejection; these should be understood.
What are the four?
Having seen a beggar, one conceives the thought of them as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and harbors no intent to harm;
one does not delight in one's own pleasure but constantly desires to bring joy to others;
and one cultivates and accumulates extensive learning without ever feeling satiated.
To extensively expound for others within the great assembly the Dharma that one has heard and retained, without expecting gain or honor—
this is the fourth. "Kinnara King!
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva accomplishes four things, they will experience anxiety and distress;
these should be recognized.
What are the four?
They do not accumulate the path of the perfections;
they do not cultivate the means of integration;
and they do not apply themselves with diligence to teaching and transforming sentient beings.
To become complacent with oneself regarding minor merits and fail to cultivate the immeasurable merits of a bodhisattva—
this is the fourth. "Kinnara King!
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who accomplishes four dharmas will be free from sorrow and distress; this should be understood.
What are the four?
They are to always apply oneself with diligent vigor in the cultivation of the various pāramitās, as if one’s head were on fire.
They constantly and diligently apply themselves to gathering the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
They constantly and diligently apply themselves to teaching and transforming sentient beings.
With diligent application, they cultivate and fulfill all merits, amassing the immeasurable merits of a bodhisattva.
"These are the four.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these four dharmas, he sent the Great Tree Kinnara King to address King Ajātaśatru:
"Great King!"
“Have you now heard this teaching on the four phrases of the bodhisattva’s sorrowless dharma?
King Ajātaśatru then addressed the Buddha, saying,
“I have heard it.”
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, Great King,
those bodhisattvas who practice for enlightenment should not be distressed.”
King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva cultivate the practice of enlightenment?”

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to fulfill the Dharma-sounds produced by the musical instruments of the *kiṃnaras*, *gandharvas*, *mahoragas*, and others, and further desiring to answer King Ajātaśatru’s inquiry regarding the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the practices for awakening, spoke these verses to clarify their meaning:
“If one wishes to cultivate beneficial practices, Having heard the Dharma, one should act according to it;
Cultivating the most supreme practice of awakening, While performing that cultivation, one remains free from sorrow or anxiety.”
They cultivate practices for peace and happiness for the sake of sentient beings, practicing equanimity and loving-kindness toward all;
they practice the supreme conduct of awakening, in which there are no various mixed types of conduct.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they cultivate steadfast practice;
those practitioners whose resolve is pure, who cultivate the most supreme conduct of bodhi—such practitioners shall never fall into the evil realms.
They cultivate the practice of giving and relinquishment, practicing the total renunciation of all things;
they practice the most supreme conduct for awakening, and such persons possess no conduct of stinginess.
Practicing the pure precepts and the conduct of tranquility, with body and speech pure and free from defilement;
practicing the most supreme conduct for awakening, they shall never at last violate the holy life.
They practice the conduct that benefits through patience, And the conduct that is free from the fault of anger;
They practice the supreme conduct of awakening, In which the poison of the fault of anger does not exist.
They practice the pillar-like conduct of the power of diligence, And practice without weariness amidst birth and death;
They practice the supreme conduct of awakening, And they never again engage in the conduct of indolence.
They cultivate the practice of meditative concentration and samādhi, with body and mind solitary and tranquil, free from clamor;
they practice the supreme conduct of bodhi, and thus they never engage in the conduct of worldly bustle.
Practicing the wisdom of the bodhisattva path, all dharmic practices are likewise so!
Practicing the most supreme conduct of enlightenment, there shall ultimately be no conduct they do not know.
They practice the beneficial conduct of a compassionate mind, And toward all sentient beings, they excel in the conduct of compassion;
They practice the supreme conduct of awakening, And they never engage in conduct that harms others.
They practice the conduct of emptiness and the conduct of tranquility; The pure conduct of signlessness and wishlessness;
They practice the supreme conduct of awakening, And ultimately have no conduct of wishing for anything.
Practicing the true path and the practice of ultimate truth, Fulfilling all-encompassing wisdom with complete practice;
Practicing the most supreme path to enlightenment, They shall ultimately never encounter any obstructive practice.
They practice the conduct of faith and the conduct of joy; they practice the conduct of virtuous reflection without distraction;
they practice the supreme conduct of awakening; they shall never engage in conduct of lack of faith.
Practicing the conduct of meditative concentration and liberation, One attains the wondrous practice of the five supernormal powers;
Practicing the most supreme conduct of bodhi, One will ultimately have no obstructed conduct.
Cultivating the conduct of the Buddhas and the conduct of the Dharma, Providing for the Sangha Jewel with pure conduct;
Practicing the most supreme conduct of Bodhi— Such a person possesses the most excellent and true practice.
They cultivate the practice of the Dharma and the practice of emptiness; they cultivate the practice of teaching and transforming all sentient beings;
they cultivate the most supreme practice of awakening, and they never have a dwelling place where they cease their progress.
Cultivating the practices of causes and the practices of karmic fruition, They sever all practices that lead to the extremes of existence;
Practicing the most supreme conduct of awakening, They ultimately possess no conduct of attachment.
They practice pure conduct and stainless conduct, And the conduct that liberates from all fetters and afflictions;
They practice the most supreme conduct of bodhi, And they never again possess conduct of feverish distress.
They cultivate the practice of peaceful liberation; They cultivate the practice of bestowing fearlessness upon all sentient beings;
They cultivate the supreme practice of awakening; They possess the practice that fulfills all vows.
Practicing the course of the sun and the course of the moon, their conduct remains unsullied like a lotus flower;
practicing the supreme conduct of awakening, they are honored and saluted by humans and devas.
He practices the conduct of Śakra and the conduct of Brahmā, To fulfill the sublime practice of pure dharmas;
He practices the most supreme conduct of bodhi, That conduct which strikes terror into the armies of Māra.
Practicing superior conduct and supreme conduct, they sever the practice of desire and hatred;
practicing the most supreme conduct of enlightenment, they shall never again have the practice of hatred or delusion.
They practice the observance of the prohibitions of non-Buddhist paths, the wondrous conduct of the pure eye of wisdom;
they practice the most supreme conduct of bodhi, and thus they ultimately possess no conduct of delusive conceptualization.
Cultivating the practice of discipline and tranquility, free from the deluded conduct of name-and-form;
practicing the supreme path to enlightenment—such a person is revered by humans and devas.
Cultivating easy practices and beneficial conduct, Severing the left-hand paths through supreme and wondrous practice;
Practicing the most excellent path to enlightenment— Such a person shall always possess the benefit of wisdom.
Practicing the courageous path and advancing with diligence, he performs the heroic deeds that terrify the armies of Māra;
practicing the supreme conduct of awakening, there is nothing on the path to the seat of enlightenment that he does not know.
Cultivating manifest conduct and conduct without concealment, One attains the wondrous practice of dhāraṇī;
Practicing the most supreme conduct of bodhi, Such a person does not lose the fruit of their practice.
They cultivate the conduct of kings and the conduct of tranquility; at all times, they practice the conduct of renunciation.
They cultivate the supreme conduct of awakening; such are their practices of acting according to what they have taught.
They cultivate the conduct of householders and superior practices, yet they engage in worldly conduct that is unsurpassed;
they cultivate practices corresponding to skillful means, yet they relinquish the subtle practices of dhyāna-bliss;
they practice the most supreme conduct for awakening, and thus they never possess conduct characterized by affliction or feverish distress.
Cultivating worldly conduct while remaining detached from worldly conduct—the practices of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm;
practicing the supreme conduct of awakening, they shall ultimately never have any fearful conduct.
Cultivating all-pervasive practices, they fulfill the faculties through skillful conduct;
practicing the supreme path to enlightenment, their wisdom is like space.
When these dharmas of the bodhisattva practices were being taught, five hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

King Ajātaśatru and his retinue, as well as eight thousand beings among the brahmins, householders, and kinnara followers in the city of Rājagṛha, having resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We shall practice the various bodhisattva practices for awakening as they have been described above, exactly as taught.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Kinnara King Mahādruma:
"You may now depart and return to your dwelling."

At that time, the Great Kinnara King Druma, together with his queen, their children, and all their retinue, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and confessed their transgressions before the World-Honored One.

As various musical instruments were played and the heavens rained down a multitude of flowers, a great radiance was emitted and the earth shook in six ways; he then immediately returned to Mount Gandhamādana.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"That the Great Tree Kinnara King is thus able to make such a true offering to the Buddha and a true offering to the Dharma.
The Buddha said, "Kauśika!"

Not only is he called "True" for your sake alone; throughout the entire trichiliocosm, among all the Śakras, Brahmās, World-Protectors, celestial kings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, this Kinnara King is truly and preeminently supreme.
Why is this? Lord of Devas!
Once a bodhisattva has resolved their mind [on awakening], they have already surpassed all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Kauśika! There is no one who can surpass a bodhisattva, with the sole exception of a Tathāgata! Why is this?
“From the Bodhisattva, the Tathāgata is born;
from the Tathāgata, all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are born.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, having heard these words from the Tathāgata, wept with streaming tears and spoke as follows:
"I have now forever departed from the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the Devaputra Gopī said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
"O Father-King, Lord of Devas!

It is so, it is so! All conditioned phenomena and all dharmas, being obscured by the arising of delusive thoughts, cannot give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; they cannot compassionately regard all sentient beings, nor can they cultivate a mind of great loving-kindness.
"Father King, Lord of Devas, why do you now say:
'Having entered the stage of right determination, his seeds are burnt and destroyed; he is forever not a vessel for this Mahāyāna'?
When the Devaputra Gopī spoke these words, five hundred devaputras among the Trāyastriṃśa gods all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At that time, the Devaputra Gopī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I wish to personally behold the practices performed by the Bodhisattva—those hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of difficult and painful austerities, up to his attainment of the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) under Dīpaṃkara Buddha. We pray that the Buddha will briefly explain this; having heard it, we shall practice as instructed so that we may attain this Dharma.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Devaputra Gopī:
"There is no bodhisattva who attains the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) without having planted roots of goodness;
only after a bodhisattva has planted immeasurable roots of goodness does he subsequently attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas."
Gopī Devaputra!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
What are the four?
All Buddhas are equal;
all dharmas are equal;
all worlds are equal.
"All sentient beings are equal, Gopī!
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena."
"Furthermore, he accomplishes four dharmas.
What are the four?
He delights in the four formless attainments."
They delight in the three gates of liberation through great compassion;
they delight in the skillful means of the six pāramitās;
and they delight in meditative concentration and the five supernormal powers.
These are the four. Furthermore, there are four other dharmas to be accomplished.
What are these four?
To understand that the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) is itself bodhi;
to know that the nature of all elements (*dhātu*) is gathered within bodhi, and to have faith that the nature of bodhi is itself the nature of the elements;
to know that the nature of all sense-bases (*āyatana*) is gathered within bodhi, and to contemplate all sense-bases through the nature of bodhi.
"All dharmas are gathered within bodhi; the nature of bodhi is itself the nature of all dharmas—of this there is no doubt.
This is the fourth.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas."
What are these four? They are:
knowing that all phenomena abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) without wavering;
and knowing that all phenomena abide within suchness (tathatā).
Because one has faith in the nature of the equality of the dharmas of the three periods of time as being indestructible;
because one contemplates all dharmas as equal, having a nature like that of space. Gopī!
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves the patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

When this teaching was spoken, five hundred bodhisattvas attained the patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena, and the devaputra Gopī attained the patient endurance of conformity (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, intending to seal this Dharma discourse, addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda!
You should receive and uphold this sutra, titled ‘The Sutra on the King of the Kinnaras, Mahādruma, Entering and Practicing All Dharma-Gates.’”
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One,
I have received and upheld it.”
It is unprecedented, World-Honored One!
This sutra is exceedingly profound and subtle; its meaning is definitive and its phrasing is magnificent.
"Bhagavān!
There is no other sūtra that can surpass this sūtra; within this very sūtra, there is nothing that is not revealed.
Bhagavān!"
I have attained the light of the Dharma before my very eyes, yet not through any other sutra than this one;
I now personally realize that within this sutra I have obtained hundreds of thousands of ten-thousands of millions of merits.
“World-Honored One!

I have now entered the stage of a śrāvaka with this limited and finite wisdom; yet, having heard this sutra, I have already attained such great illumination of the Dharma. How much more so for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has perfected the vessel of the immeasurable great ocean, who cultivates and accumulates all dharmas through fearless great wisdom, and who acts as an uninvited friend to all sentient beings—how many dharma-gates would such a one of immeasurable great wisdom attain upon hearing a teaching such as this?”
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!

If all the light of the suns and moons throughout this trichiliocosm were compared to the light of the Dharma attained by these bodhisattvas, the light from a single pore of their skin would completely eclipse all that light of the suns and moons."
Ānanda! If the Buddha-Tathāgata emits light from all his pores, these lights are all endowed with wisdom. Why is this?
Because all that the Buddha possesses is wisdom. Ānanda!
The Tathāgata possesses this light of wisdom; by means of this light of wisdom, the Tathāgata is able to know the mental activities of all sentient beings.
If there are sentient beings who hear this sutra, they shall all attain this great wisdom and luminous illumination;

if they copy it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it until they master it, explain it extensively for others among the great assembly, contemplate it with right mindfulness, and practice according to its teachings, such persons shall never depart from the bodhicitta. Adorned with great compassion in teaching and transforming sentient beings, they don the armor of great loving-kindness to eliminate all demons.
"Ānanda, you should know that such a person will certainly proceed to the site of enlightenment.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
By the power of the Buddha, I have now received and upheld this sutra-dharma.
World-Honored One!
If there are good men or good women who...
“If one upholds this sutra, recites it, copies it, and extensively explains it for others among the great assembly, how much merit will they obtain?
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
If there is a bodhisattva, a son of good family, or a daughter of good family, who, during the first part of the day,

gives all the seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm as a gift to srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, and all pratyekabuddhas, up to and including all Buddhas— and likewise during the middle part of the day, the evening, and throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night— performing such giving for a full thousand years.
Ānanda! What do you think?
Regarding these sons and daughters of good family!
“Would the merit thus obtained be great?
“It would be very great,
World-Honored One!”
"Very much so,
Sugata! World-Honored One!"
"If the merit obtained in a single day is immeasurable and boundless, how much more so after a thousand years?
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
I now proclaim to these sons and daughters of good family:

for those who, seeking awakening, seeking to transform sentient beings, and seeking to turn the wheel of Dharma, receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and extensively manifest this sutra within the great assembly, their merit shall be supreme; how much more so for those who are further able to practice according to the teaching?
Ānanda! If one receives, maintains, and even recites a single four-line verse from this sutra and explains it extensively for others in the great assembly, their merit shall be superior.
Why is this? Such giving is called the gift of Dharma, the most supreme among all gifts.
This kind of giving is precisely the gift of Dharma; it is the supreme relinquishment, namely, the relinquishing of the Dharma.
This is called the supreme reception, meaning the reception of the Dharma;
this is called the supreme upholding, meaning the upholding of the Dharma. Why is this so?

Ānanda! The gift of the Dharma can extinguish the fetters and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), whereas the gift of material wealth increases afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, a bodhisattva, in order to extinguish the fetters and underlying tendencies, should practice the gift of the Dharma; this is what the Buddha has authorized. Such a gift of the Dharma is able to encompass all merits.
“Ānanda! There are thirty-two meritorious titles for the Dharma-giving of a bodhisattva.
What are these thirty-two?
There is right mindfulness;
there is wisdom; there is progress.
There are those who are free from the fetter of stinginess;
there are those with little sensual desire;
and there are those with little ill will.
Possessing but slight ignorance,
he has subdued all fetters and afflictions of both himself and others;
he is beloved and respected by many people and praised by the devas.
Various nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others will constantly follow and protect them.
They will unfailingly enjoy the offerings of humans—
clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine— obtaining these without having to seek them.
His fame shall spread far and wide;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, no malevolent spirits or ghosts shall find an opportunity to harm him,
and he shall be praised by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
They shall protect the true Dharma and uphold the treasury of the Buddha’s teachings;
they will not fall into any of the evil realms,
and it will not be difficult for them to be reborn among humans or devas.
They are never apart from seeing the Buddha;
they are never apart from hearing the Dharma;
they are never apart from making offerings to the Sangha.
They shall attain the recollection of past lives,
be born in pure Buddha-fields,
and in every place of birth, their sense faculties shall be complete.
One attains a body adorned with the thirty-two marks, becoming a supreme lord;
one plants the fundamental seeds of dhāraṇī and creates the causes for uninterrupted eloquence and wisdom.
One gains the company of wise people;
by accumulating the causes of great wisdom,
one swiftly attains the Dharma and does not give rise to thoughts of improper mindfulness.
Having relinquished all worldly material gifts,
one attains the great treasury of Dharma and inexhaustible eloquence. Ānanda!
“The Dharma-giving of a bodhisattva possesses these thirty-two merits and renown.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
We, too, shall receive and uphold this sutra.
World-Honored One!

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there will be sentient beings who are vessels for the Dharma; we vow that they shall hear this sutra, and we shall cause them to believe and understand it, and we shall protect them.
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
We desire to attain the merits mentioned above.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Excellent, excellent,
O Lord of Devas!"
It is well that you are now able to diligently protect the Dharma and let out the lion’s roar.
Lord of Devas!
By these roots of goodness from protecting the Dharma, as long as my Dharma remains, the hosts of asuras shall all be subdued and the devas shall attain victory.
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because one attains the vision of such a fearless dharma, namely, being without any defilement or attachment toward all dharmas.
"Lord of Devas!
All fears whatsoever arise from dwelling in attachment to the view of a self.
Lord of Devas!"
"If one is without attachment, this is the protection of the True Dharma.
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
I, too, shall renounce immeasurable dhyāna-pleasures and travel to various cities, towns, villages, and districts to circulate this Dharma;
I shall also go there to listen to the Dharma, so that the teacher of the Dharma may attain firm power of mindfulness.
"Why is this? From within this Dharma, there arise immeasurable śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, Śakras, Brahmās, and Lokapālas.
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We, the four kings, shall firmly protect these Buddhas and their śrāvakas, so that this Dharma of the sutra may endure for a long time. If any among our retinues do not believe in this Dharma of the Buddha, we shall subdue them and cause them to believe; they shall then apply themselves with diligent vigor within the Buddha-Dharma, drawing near to it with affection and joy.”
"Bhagavān!
If there are devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, or others who harbor evil intentions, and one wishes to subdue them, one should recite this mantra."
That is to say:
"1. Tārabī; 2. Śrībī."
Śivāśivāhulu.

"By the spiritual power of this mantra, all who seek to find fault shall be completely subdued. (21) At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, Tianguan Bodhisattva, and all the virtuous men:

"I now entrust to you this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, which was accumulated over immeasurable thousands of millions of asamkhyeya kalpas and is difficult to obtain, so that it may endure for a long time without interruption or extinction."
Then Maitreya Bodhisattva and Devamauli Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

After the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, we shall widely disseminate this Dharma of the sutra so that it may come into the hands of all bodhisattvas who have planted deep roots of goodness and all sentient beings alike. We shall enable them to attain mastery over it, subdue their pride, and be able to uphold this sutra with faith, aspiration, and understanding.”

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if there are those who hear this sutra-dharma, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, copy it, or explain it, you should know that they are all sustained by the spiritual power of Maitreya Bodhisattva and Devaputra-crown Bodhisattva.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas came into the assembly and said:
"World-Honored One!
Regarding the various dharmas spoken for the sake of the śrāvakas, not even a single hair of mine would stand on end."
Now the World-Honored One expounds such Dharma of the bodhisattva path, sealed with the seal of the bodhisattvas and sustained by the Tathāgata, to which all sentient beings turn for refuge.
While you were preaching such a Dharma, we have now been struck by the arrow of sorrow; we know for ourselves that we are already subject to birth and old age.
We pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will take our hands and no longer expound this Sūtra of the Power of Such Great Merit, lest we be pierced again by the arrow of sorrow.
The Buddha said to Pāpīyas:
"Do not grieve; there are many sentient beings within your realm who do not believe in this sutra, while only a few sentient beings are able to believe and accept it."

Pāpīyān, you should know that those sentient beings who have faith in this profound Dharma are as few as the small amount of soil one might grasp from the great earth; those who do not have faith are as numerous as the rest of the great earth.
Pāpīyan! Those who lack faith are all your followers; therefore, Pāpīyan, you should feel joy. Pāpīyan!
“The realm of sentient beings is immeasurable and boundless.

When this Dharma was spoken, immeasurable sentient beings dwelt in the mind of unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment; ninety-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas; eighty-four thousand sentient beings were freed from dust and defilement and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; and eight thousand bhikṣus, having exhausted all outflows, attained liberation of mind.

At that time, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways; a great light shone everywhere, and the heavens rained down various flowers. Hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck. Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of devas leaped for joy and praised with songs and hymns, exclaiming:
"Today, within Jambudvīpa, we behold the Wheel of Dharma turning once again!"
The World-Honored One previously turned the wheel of the true Dharma in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, benefiting sentient beings;
now, by preaching this sutra, he benefits sentient beings—this is what makes it superior.
"Any sentient being who upholds this sutra will, before long, turn the wheel of Dharma.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Devanetra Bodhisattva, the Venerable Ānanda, and others addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What should this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! This sutra is titled ‘The Questions of the Kinnara King Mahādruma,’ and it is also titled ‘The Chapter on Proclaiming the Inconceivable Dharma.’”
"Thus should it be upheld.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Devatāmukuṭa Bodhisattva, the Venerable Ānanda, and the entire great assembly—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas—having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all filled with great joy.
